english: Some things are so great, so far beyond man — so far past what our mortal nature can reach — that our rational and dying race cannot possibly grasp them. Yet they become possible when God pours out his grace upon men, great grace beyond measure, through Jesus Christ, the servant of his unsurpassable grace toward us, and through the co-working Spirit — all by the will of God.

Take the possession of Wisdom, by whom all things were made — for, as David says, in wisdom God made them all. For human nature as it stands this is impossible; yet out of the impossible it becomes possible, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who became wisdom to us from God — righteousness and sanctification and redemption.

For what man shall know the counsel of God? Or who shall conceive what the Lord wills? Since the reasonings of mortals are timid, and our notions insecure. For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthy tent burdens a mind crowded with cares. Hardly do we guess at the things on earth — but the things in heaven, who has ever traced them out?

Who would deny that it is impossible for a man to trace out the things in heaven? And yet even this impossible thing becomes possible by God's surpassing grace. For the one who was caught up to the third heaven perhaps did trace out the things in the three heavens — since he had heard unspeakable words, which no man is permitted to utter.

Who could say it is possible for a man to come to know the mind of the Lord? Yet even this God grants through Christ. [Here the chief manuscript has a gap of about three and a half lines, which held a discussion of the words in John 15; the conjectural fillings proposed by editors are not rendered as Origen's text.]

But as no one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man within him, so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. And if no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, it is impossible for a man to know the things of God. Consider too how even this becomes possible. We, he says, received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, that we might know the things freely given us by God — things we speak not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit (Titus 3:5–6) (Psalm 104:24) (1 Corinthians 1:30) (Wisdom 9:13–16) (2 Corinthians 12:2) (2 Corinthians 12:4) (Romans 11:34) (1 Corinthians 2:16) (1 Corinthians 2:11) (1 Corinthians 2:12–13).

title: Grace makes the impossible possible

english: But it is likely, most God-fearing and industrious Ambrose, and most modest and courageous Tatiana — from whom, I pray, womanly frailty has already departed, as it had departed from Sarah — that you wonder why, when our treatise concerns prayer, these opening remarks have been about things impossible for men but made possible by God's grace. What I am persuaded of is this: that to expound the whole subject of prayer exactly and worthily of God — both how one must pray, and what to say to God in prayer, and which times are fitter than other times for prayer — is, given our weakness, one of those impossibilities. [Here T has illegible letters, probably a further elaboration.]

The one of these, then — I mean the 'what' — is the words of prayer; the 'how' is the disposition of the one who prays. For example, of the 'what': Ask for the great things, and the small shall be added to you; and ask for the heavenly things, and the earthly shall be added to you; and pray for those who persecute you; and beg the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into his harvest; and pray that you may not enter into temptation. Of the 'how': pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath; and in praying, do not babble; and whatever resembles these. Of the 'how' again: I desire then that men pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger and doubting; and likewise that women adorn themselves in modest dress, with shame and self-control, not with braids or gold or pearls or costly clothing, but — as befits women professing godliness — with good works. Instructive of the 'how' is also this: if you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first be reconciled to your brother, and then come offer your gift. For what greater gift can be sent up to God from a rational being than the fragrant word of prayer, offered from a conscience bearing no stench of sin? Further of the 'how': do not deprive one another, except by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer, and come together again, lest Satan test you for your lack of self-control. For the 'how' is hindered by these things, unless even the act of the marriage mysteries — things fit to be passed over in silence — becomes more solemn and slower and more passionless, when the harmony named here dissolves passion's dissonance and consumes intemperance and checks Satan's malicious gloating. Besides, instructive of the 'how' is this: whenever you stand praying, forgive whatever you hold against anyone. And Paul's word: every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head; but every woman praying or prophesying with her head unveiled dishonors her own head. You illustrate the 'how.'

But Paul knew all these things, and many times more from the Law and the prophets and the fullness of the Gospel, which he could set forth with varied exposition of each — and he speaks from a disposition not merely moderate but truthful. Yet seeing, beyond all this, how far short we fall of knowing what to pray as we ought — but what to pray as we ought, we do not know — he adds to his treatise the source from which the lack is filled: for the one who does not know, yet has made himself worthy to have the lack filled in him. For he says that the Spirit itself intercedes with unutterable groanings; and he who searches hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, for he intercedes for saints according to God. And the Spirit crying Abba, Father in the hearts of the blessed, which knows well the groans in the tent — groans [obscure clause, see note] the fallen and transgressors — intercedes with God with unutterable groanings, taking up our groans in great love for man and sympathy. And seeing in its wisdom our soul humbled to dust and confined in the body of humiliation, it intercedes with God not with just any groans but with certain unutterable ones, akin to the unspeakable words which no man may utter. This Spirit, then, not content with that for which it intercedes with God, straining its intercession on our behalf — concerning, I think, the more-than-conquerors, like the one who says, In all these things we are more than conquerors. And it is likely that it intercedes only for those not so great as to be more than conquerors, nor again such as to be conquered, but for conquerors.

Next, attached to 'but what to pray as we ought, we do not know, but the Spirit intercedes with unutterable groanings' (Genesis 18:11) is 'I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also.' (Matthew 6:33) For our mind cannot pray unless the Spirit first prays, as in accompaniment of it — just as it cannot sing and hymn the Father in Christ rhythmically, melodiously, metrically, harmoniously, unless the Spirit who searches all things, even the depths of God, first praises and hymns him whose depths it has searched and, as far as it could, grasped.

But I think some one of Jesus' disciples, sensing human weakness — falling short of how one ought to pray — and realizing this especially when he heard learned and great discourses uttered by the Savior in his prayer to the Father, said to the Lord when he stopped praying: Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples. The whole sequence of the saying runs thus: And it came to pass, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said to him: Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples to pray. For would a man reared on the Law's catechism, hearing the prophetic readings, never missing the synagogues, not have known how to pray at all until he saw the Lord praying in a certain place? To say so is absurd. He prayed according to Jewish custom, of course — but he saw that he needed a greater knowledge for prayer's ground. And what did John teach his disciples about prayer — they who came to be baptized by him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the countryside — if he did not see something more than a prophet concerning prayer, which [here T has a gap of about two lines, perhaps holding Matthew 3:5-6] it is likely he delivered not to all the baptized but in secret to those being discipled toward baptism? Such prayers, truly spiritual — the Spirit praying in the saints' hearts — were written down, full of secret and marvelous doctrines. In First Kingdoms, Hannah's prayer is partly recorded — for the whole of it, when she multiplied praying before the Lord, speaking in her heart, was not written down — and among the Psalms the sixteenth is entitled A prayer of David, and the eighty-ninth A prayer of Moses, the man of God, and the hundred and first A prayer of the afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his petition before the Lord. These prayers, since they truly were prayers, spoken in the Spirit and full of the doctrines of God's wisdom — one might say of the promises in them: Who is wise and will understand these things? And discerning, and will know them?

Since, then, expounding prayer is so great a task that we need the Father who also illuminates for this, and the firstborn Word himself teaching, and the Spirit empowering, to conceive and speak worthily of so great a proposal — having prayed as a man (for I hardly grant myself to contain prayer), I ask to obtain, before the treatise, the Spirit's prayer: that a most full and spiritual discourse may be granted us, and the prayers recorded in the Gospels clarified. We must now begin the treatise on prayer (Luke 12:31) (Luke 6:28) (Matthew 9:38) (Luke 22:40) (Matthew 24:20) (Matthew 6:7) (1 Timothy 2:8–10) (Matthew 5:23–24) (1 Corinthians 7:5) (Mark 11:25) (1 Corinthians 11:4–5) (Romans 8:26) (Romans 8:27) (Romans 8:15) (Romans 8:37) (2 Corinthians 12:4) (1 Corinthians 14:14–15) (1 Corinthians 2:10) (Luke 11:1) (1 Samuel 1:12–13) (Hosea 14:10) (Colossians 1:15) (Hebrews 1:6) (Romans 8:26–27).

english: First, the name 'vow' — as far as my observation finds it placed — when Jacob, fleeing his brother Esau's wrath, [went] to Mesopotamia at Isaac and Rebekah's charges. The wording runs thus: And Jacob vowed a vow, saying: If the Lord God is with me, and keeps me in this way I go, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to put on, and brings me back safely to my father's house — then the Lord shall be my God, and this stone I set up as a pillar shall be God's house, and of all You give me I will tithe to You.

Next, note that the name εὐχή is taken — though in many places different from προσευχή — for one who promises with a vow to do certain things, if he obtains certain things from God. It is also classed among the terms of our customary speech, as we found in Exodus: after the frog plague, second in order of the ten: Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: Pray for me to the Lord, and let him take the frogs from me and my people; and I will send the people, and they shall sacrifice to the Lord. If anyone distrusts because 'pray' is Pharaoh's voice, [noting] that by 'prayer' is signified besides the former also ... [here T has illegible letters, where Origen perhaps added another similar example].

We have observed that at the gnats, the third plague, neither does Pharaoh ask that prayer be made nor does Moses pray. And at the dog-fly, the fourth, he says: Pray therefore for me to the Lord — at which Moses said: I will go out from you and pray to God, and the dog-fly shall depart from Pharaoh and his servants and his people tomorrow. And a little later: And Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to God. Again, at the fifth and sixth plagues, with neither Pharaoh asking that prayer be made nor Moses praying, at the seventh Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them: I have sinned now; the Lord is righteous, but I and my people are godless. Pray therefore to the Lord, and let there cease to be voices of God and hail and fire. And a little later: And Moses went out from Pharaoh, outside the city, and spread out his hands to the Lord, and the voices ceased. Why it is not said 'and he prayed,' as with the former, but 'he spread out his hands to the Lord,' (Genesis 28:20–22) must be examined more opportunely elsewhere. And at the eighth plague Pharaoh says: Pray then to the Lord your God, and let him take this death from me. And Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to God.

In many places, we have said, the name εὐχή is placed not in the customary way as with Jacob. In Leviticus too: And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and you shall say to them: A man or woman who vows a great vow to purify purity to the Lord shall purify himself from wine and strong drink — and what follows about the one who wishes to be a Nazirite; then a little later: And he shall sanctify his head in that day, on which he was sanctified to the Lord for the days of the vow. And again a little later: This is the law of the one who vowed: on whatever day he fulfills a day of his vow; and again a little on: And after this the vowed one shall drink wine. This is the law of the one who vowed, who vows to the Lord his gift concerning the vow, besides what his hand finds, according to the power of his vow, which he vowed according to the law of purity. And toward the end of Numbers: And Moses spoke to the rulers of the tribes of the children of Israel, saying: This is the word the Lord commanded: A man who vows a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath with a definition, or defines concerning his soul, shall not profane his word; all that comes out of his mouth he shall do. But if a woman vows a vow to the Lord or defines a definition in her father's house in her youth, and her father hears her vows and her definitions which she defined against her soul, and her father keeps silence — all her vows shall stand, and all the definitions which she defined against her soul shall remain for her — and in sequence with these he lays down certain laws about such. According to this signification it is written in Proverbs: [here T has a gap of about 110 letters; 'a snare' is certain, two further sayings conjectured] A snare to a man to consecrate hastily anything of his own; for after vowing comes repenting. And in Ecclesiastes: It is good not to vow than to vow and not pay. And in the Acts of the Apostles: There are four men with us, having a vow of themselves (Genesis 27:42–28:2) (Exodus 8:8–9) (Exodus 8:16–19) (Exodus 8:25–30) (Exodus 9:27–28) (Exodus 9:33) (Exodus 10:16–18) (Leviticus 27:1–8) (Numbers 6:2–3) (Numbers 6:11–13) (Numbers 6:20–21) (Numbers 30:2–6) (Proverbs 20:25) (Ecclesiastes 5:3–4) (Acts 21:23) (Exodus 8:8–10:18) (Numbers 6:2–21).

english: It seemed to me not unreasonable first to distinguish what is signified in Scripture, since εὐχή signifies two things — and likewise προσευχή. For this name, besides its common and customary use in many places, is also placed for what we customarily mean by εὐχή, as in the Hannah passages in First Kingdoms: And Eli the priest sat on a throne at the doorposts of the temple of the Lord. And she, bitter in soul, prayed to the Lord and wept weeping. And she vowed a vow and said: O Lord of hosts, if in oversight You look upon Your servant's humiliation and remember me and do not forget Your servant, and give Your servant a male seed — I will give him to the Lord as a gift all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head.

One might not unreasonably say here, attending to 'she prayed to the Lord' (Leviticus 27:1–8) and 'she vowed a vow': if she did both — that is, she prayed to the Lord and she vowed a vow — perhaps 'she prayed' is placed for what we customarily call prayer, while 'she vowed a vow' is placed for what is signified as ordered in Leviticus and Numbers. For 'I will give him to the Lord as a gift all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head' (1 Samuel 1:9–11) is not strictly prayer but that vow — like Jephthah's in these words: And Jephthah vowed a vow to the Lord and said: If You deliver the Ammonites into my hand, then whoever comes out of my house's doors to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the Lord's, and I will offer him as a burnt offering (Numbers 6:2–3) (Judges 11:30–31).

english: If then we must next, as you ordered, set forth first the plausible arguments of those who think nothing is accomplished by prayers, and therefore say praying is superfluous, we shall not hesitate to do this too as we can — since the name of prayer is now used by us more commonly and simply [here T has illegible letters]. This doctrine, then, is inglorious and without distinguished patrons, so that you can hardly find anyone who accepts providence and sets God over all things yet rejects prayer. For the doctrine belongs either to outright atheists who deny God's very substance, or to those who honor God as far as the name goes but rob him of providence. Already the opposing activity — wanting to drape the most godless doctrines with Christ's name and the Son of God's teaching — has managed to persuade some of its view; its leaders abolish all sensibles entirely, using neither baptism nor eucharist, slandering the Scriptures as though even 'to pray' were not their will but they taught something else than this.

The arguments of the prayer-rejecters would run thus — those, that is, who set God over all and say there is providence (for we need not now examine what is said by those who wholly abolish God or providence): God knows all things before their birth, and nothing ever comes to be known by him for the first time, as previously unknown. [Here T is illegible; the editors conjecture mockery of prayers and total rejection.] What need is there, then, to send up prayer to one who knows our needs before we pray? For your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask him. And it is reasonable that he, being father and maker of all, loving all beings and loathing nothing he made, should arrange each one's affairs savingly even without prayer — like a father presiding over infants who cannot ask at all, or who in ignorance often want the opposite of what helps and profits. But men fall shorter of God than mere babes fall short of their parents' minds.

It is likely that God not only foreknew what will be but also predetermined it, and nothing happens beyond what was predetermined. Just as if someone prayed for the sun to rise he would be thought a fool — asking by prayer for what will be even without his prayer — so a man would be senseless who thinks that by his prayer come things that would wholly be even if he had not prayed. And again: as he surpasses all madness who, troubled by the sun in the summer solstice and burning, thinks to move the sun by prayer to the spring signs to enjoy temperate air — so whoever thinks he will escape the necessary accidents of the human race by praying would surpass all melancholy.

And if sinners were estranged from the womb, and the righteous one set apart from his mother's belly — and when they were not yet born nor had done anything good or bad, that God's elective purpose might stand, not of works but of him who calls, it is said: the elder shall serve the younger — we ask forgiveness of sins in vain, or to receive a spirit of power with Christ empowering us. For if we are sinners, we were estranged from the womb; but if we were set apart from our mother's belly, the best will meet even those who do not pray. For what prayer did Jacob offer, before being born, to be prophesied superior to Esau, and his brother to serve him? What impiety did Esau commit to be hated before birth? Why does Moses pray — as found in the eighty-ninth Psalm — if God is his refuge before the mountains were settled and the earth and world were formed?

But also concerning all who shall be saved, it is written in Ephesians that the Father chose them in him, in Christ, before the foundation of the world, that they be holy and blameless before him, in love predestining them to adoption through Christ to himself. Either one is among those elect before the foundation, and cannot fall from election — so no need of prayer for him — or one is not elect nor predestined, and prays in vain: though he pray myriad times, he shall not be heard. For whom God foreknew, these he also predestined conformed to the image of the glory of his Son; and whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also glorified. Why does Josiah toil, or why does he in prayer care whether he shall be heard or not — prophesied by name generations before, and foretold not only foreknown but proclaimed to many ears what he would do? Why does Judas pray — so that his prayer become sin — proclaimed since David's times as one who would lose his overseership, with another taking it instead? [Here T has a gap of about 100 letters.] It of itself shows: with God unchangeable, comprehending all beforehand, abiding in what was predetermined — to pray thinking to turn his purpose by prayer, or approaching as one who did not predetermine but waits for each one's prayer, so that through prayer he may ordain what befits the pray-er — making him deem reasonable only then what is under scrutiny, having not observed it before. [Closing obscure; see note.]

Let there lie before us in their own words what you set out in your letter, thus: First, if God foreknows the future and they must happen, prayer is vain. Second, if all things happen by God's will, and his counsels are unmoved, and nothing he wills can be turned, prayer is vain. These, I think, are useful to assume beforehand toward dissolving the arguments that hold men back from praying (Matthew 6:8) (Wisdom 11:24) (Psalm 58:3) (Galatians 1:15) (Romans 9:11–13) (Genesis 25:23) (Romans 9:13) (Psalm 90:2) (Ephesians 1:4–5) (Romans 8:29–30) (1 Kings 13:2) (Psalm 109:7–8) (Acts 1:20).

english: Of things moved, some have their mover from outside — like lifeless things held together by mere habit, and things moved by nature and soul: not as such ever moved thus, but like things held by habit alone. For stones and wood, cut from the mine or having lost the growing, held by habit alone, have their mover from outside; and animals' bodies too, and portable plants, when shifted by something — not as animals and plants, but like stones and wood that lost growing. And though even these move, since all wasting bodies are in flux, their movement in wasting is consequential. Second beyond these are things moved by indwelling nature or soul — which are said to be moved from themselves by those who use names strictly. Third is the movement in animals, called movement from themselves. And the movement of rationals, I think, is movement through themselves. Remove self-movement from an animal and it can no longer be conceived as still an animal, but will be like a plant moved by nature alone or a stone carried from outside. And if something follows upon its own movement — since we named this 'being moved from itself' (Galatians 1:15) — it must be rational.

Those who want nothing to be up to us will necessarily admit most absurd things: first, that we are not animals; second, that we are not even rational — but as though moved by an outside mover, ourselves in no way moving, we are said by it to do what we are thought to do. Besides, let anyone attend to his own affections and see whether he will shamelessly say: it is not I who will, not I who eat, not I who walk, not I who assent and accept whatever doctrines, not I who nod toward others away from false ones. As it is impossible for a man to be disposed toward certain doctrines, though he invent myriad times with plausible arguments, so it is impossible to be disposed about human affairs as if the 'up to us' were in no way preserved. For who is disposed that nothing is graspable, or so lives as suspending judgment on everything whatsoever? Who does not rebuke his servant, having taken an impression of the servant's fault? Who does not accuse a son who fails his duty to parents, or blame and censure one who did shameful things, or the adulterous wife? For truth forces and compels, even though one invent myriad times, to rouse(?) and praise and blame — with the 'up to us' preserved, and what depends on us becoming praiseworthy or blameworthy.

If then the 'up to us' is preserved — having countless turnings toward virtue or vice, and again toward duty or against duty — necessarily this too, with the rest, before it happens, is known to God from creation and the world's foundation, of what sort it shall be. And in all things God predetermines, following what he has seen concerning each work of the 'up to us,' predetermining worthily for each 'up to us' movement what shall meet it from providence — and further, what shall come to pass in the sequence of future things. God's foreknowledge does not become the cause of all future things, even those to be effected from the 'up to us' according to our impulse. For even if, hypothetically, God did not know the future, we would not for that reason lose acting these things and willing those; rather, from foreknowledge comes this: that each one's 'up to us' takes order into the whole's administration, needful for the world's constitution.

If then each 'up to us' is known to him, and for this reason, as foreseen by him, providence dispenses worthily to each — it is reasonable also that what one prays, and with what disposition so-and-so believing thus and wanting this to happen to him, is grasped beforehand. And with this grasped, something like this will fittingly be ordered in the dispensation: 'This one praying wisely I shall hear — the very prayer he will pray; but this one I shall not hear, either because he is unworthy to be heard or because he prayed for things neither profitable for the pray-er to receive nor fitting for me to grant.' (1 Kings 13:2) 'And for this prayer, say, of so-and-so, I shall not hear him; but for that one I shall hear him.' (2 Kings 23:4–25) If anyone is troubled that God, foreknowing the future, cannot lie — as if things were necessitated — tell him that this very thing is known to God unchangeably: that this one wills the better irrevocably and firmly, or will will the worse so as to admit no change toward the profitable. And again: 'Certain things I shall do for this one praying — for it befits me, since he prays to me not blameworthily nor carelessly conducting himself about prayer. But for this one praying in measure I shall give beyond what he asks or conceives(?) certain things — for it befits me to outdo him in benefactions and supply more than he had room to ask. And to this one, who will be such, I shall send this angel as minister, from this time beginning to co-work his salvation until this time; but to this one, say, one worthier than this one, since he will be better. But from this one, after giving himself to excellent words then slipping and running back to the more material, I shall withdraw this better co-worker. And with him gone, accordingly a worse power, finding opportunity, shall mount his laziness, set upon certain sins — since he gave himself ready to sin — and provoke him.' (Psalm 109:1)

Thus then already, as it were, shall he who predetermines all things say: 'Amos shall beget Josiah, who shall not emulate his father's faults but, meeting this road urging to virtue through these companions, shall be noble and good; who shall demolish Jeroboam's ill-built altar.' And I know Judas: with my Son visiting mankind, good and noble at first, later to turn aside and fall into human sins — whom it shall be reasonable to suffer certain things for these. This foreknowledge is perhaps concerning all, but certainly concerning Judas and other mysteries, and comes in the Son of God, who saw by comprehension of the unrolling(?) of future things Judas and the sins to be sinned by him — so that after seizing(?) him, and before Judas came to be, through David he said: O God, do not pass over my praise in silence — and what follows. Knowing the future, and what tension Paul shall have toward godliness — I, before founding the world, laying down the beginning of world-making, shall choose him, and with these powers co-working human salvation set him beside them as soon as born, setting him apart from his mother's womb, permitting at first in youth with ignorant zeal, on pretext of godliness, to persecute those who believed in my Christ and to guard the garments of those stoning my servant and witness Stephen — so that later, taking occasion and changing to the better, he may not boast before me but say: I am not fit to be called apostle, because I persecuted God's church; and sensing my future benefaction to him after youthful godly-pretext faults, he may say: By God's grace I am what I am; and, checked by conscience for what in youth befell him against Christ, he may not be lifted up by the exceeding greatness of the revelations to be manifested to him for benefaction (Acts 7:58) (1 Corinthians 15:9) (1 Corinthians 15:10) (2 Corinthians 12:7) (1 Corinthians 15:9–10).

translator_notes: 'Up to us' is kept throughout for ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν (never 'free will'), matching the book's glossary; αὐτεξούσιον does not occur here.
The three movements (§1) parallel De Principiis III.1 (noted in Koetschau's apparatus); the same school vocabulary (ὁρμή, φαντασία, συγκατάθεσις implied) serves both.
§3's hypothetical ('even if God did not foreknow') is the load-bearing anti-fatalist move: foreknowledge orders freedom into providence; it does not cause.
§4-5 render God's predetermining speech in the first person, as Origen stages it (prosopopoeia), including graduated answers, angel assignments, and the withdrawn co-worker.
ὁρμᾶν (§2, 'rouse?'), the adulteress clause's joint, ἐξελιγμός ('unrolling?'), and several §4 superlatives are flagged as scan-rough; the arguments they carry are secure.

title: Prayer, providence, and how things are moved

english: And regarding prayer for the sun to rise, this must be said. There is something up to even the sun, with it praising God together with the moon — praise him, it says, sun and moon. And evidently the moon's too, and consequently all the stars': for praise him, it says, all stars and light.

As we said God uses each earthly one's 'up to us' for some earthly need, appointing them fittingly, so we must suppose he appointed the whole heavenly world and the stars' harmonious course and motion for the whole by the sun and moon and stars' 'up to us' — untransgressing(?) and firm and stable(?) and wise. And if I pray not in vain concerning another's 'up to us,' much more concerning the 'up to us' of the stars dancing in heaven savingly for the whole. Though one may say of earthly things that certain impressions arising from surroundings provoke our instability or our better-inclining to do or say this or that — but for the heavenly, what arising impression could dislodge and shift, from its world-beneficial course, each of those having such a soul fitted by reason, with motion from their own cause(?) and using such an aetherial, purest body (Psalm 148:3)?

added_allusions.reason: Praise him sun and moon; all stars and light.

translator_notes: The sunrise objection (ch. V §3) is answered cosmologically: heavenly bodies have their own ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν, stable and wise — praying 'concerning' them is not moving them like the solstice fool.
ἀπαραβάτῳ/σταθερῷ and the self-cause clause are scan-rough; the argument (stable heavenly freedom) is secure.
title: Sun, moon, and creation’s praise

english: Still, it is not unreasonable to employ such an example too, to urge toward praying and deter from neglecting prayer. As there is no begetting children without a wife and the activity taken up for childbearing, so one would not obtain certain things without having so prayed — [obscure clause] with such disposition, believing thus, not having so lived before prayer. One must not babble, then, nor ask small things, nor pray about earthly things, nor come to prayer with anger and troubled reasonings; nor without purity can one conceive leisure arising for prayer; nor can the pray-er obtain forgiveness of sins without heartily forgiving the brother who wronged him and asks pardon.

I hold that benefit comes in many ways to one who prays as one ought, or hastens toward it as he can. First, in any case, he who set his mind toward praying is benefited: by the very condition in praying he presents himself to God, and forms himself to speak to him as present — as overseeing and present. For as such impressions and reminders of certain things defile, concerning the things of which they are reminders, the reasonings born in those impressions — so we must be persuaded it is profitable to remember the believed God who observes the movements in the soul's sanctuary, with remembrance ordering itself to please him as present and overseeing, who reaches before every mind, who examines hearts and searches kidneys. For even if, hypothetically, no further benefit came to one who set his reasoning to pray beyond this one, no small thing must be conceived gained by one who thus reverently ordered himself in prayer's hour. What sins this oft-done thing keeps off, and to what right deeds it bears — those know by experience who gave themselves more constantly to praying. For if reminding and recalling a sensible man profited in wisdom provokes us to zeal for him and often blocks impulses to the worse — how much more does reminding of God, the Father of all, with prayer to him, profit those who persuaded themselves that they stand by and speak to a present and hearing God (Matthew 6:7) (Matthew 6:12) (Psalm 7:10)?

title: Why prayer is still required

english: What was said must be proved from the divine Scriptures in this way. The pray-er must lift holy hands by forgiving each who wronged him — expunging anger's passion from the soul and being angry at none. Again, lest the mind be clouded by other reasonings, one must forget all outside prayer in the hour one prays — and how is such a one not most blessed? — as Paul teaches in First Timothy, saying: I desire then that men pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger and disputes. Besides, the wife praying must especially have the restrained and modest, soul and body — above all when she prays revering God, exiling every unchaste and womanly reminder from the ruling part, adorned not with braids and gold or pearls or costly clothing, but as befits a woman professing godliness (I wonder if one would hesitate to call blessed, from this condition alone, her who so presented herself to pray) — as Paul taught in the same epistle, saying: Women likewise in modest dress, with shame and self-control adorning themselves, not with braids and gold or pearls or costly clothing, but, as befits women professing godliness, with good works.

The prophet David too says the saint praying has many other things — and these must be seasonably set beside: that what most profits may become evident, even if alone it aids(?) — what disposition and preparation for praying of one who dedicated himself to God. He says: To You I lifted my eyes, who dwell in heaven; and To You I lifted my soul, O God. For eyes of the mind, lifted from dwelling on earthly things and being filled with impressions from the more material, and raised so high as even to peer beyond creatures, coming to conceive God alone and converse solemnly and befittingly with the Hearer — how have they not already greatly profited, with unveiled face mirroring the Lord's glory, being transformed into the same image from glory to glory? Partaking then of some diviner intelligible effluence — declared by The light of Your face was signed upon us, Lord. And the soul lifted, following the Spirit, separated from body — not only following the Spirit but becoming in it — declared by To You I lifted my soul: how, already laying aside being soul, does it not become spiritual?

If forgetfulness of wrongs is a greatest feat — with the prophet Jeremiah summing the whole Law in it, saying: Not these things did I command your fathers when they went out of Egypt, but this I commanded: let each not remember his neighbor's evil in his heart — coming from forgetfulness of wrongs to prayer, we keep the Savior's command, saying: Whenever you stand praying, forgive whatever you hold against anyone. Evidently, standing thus to pray, we already possess the best (1 Timothy 2:8) (1 Timothy 2:9–10) (Psalm 123:1) (Psalm 25:1) (2 Corinthians 3:18) (Psalm 4:6) (Jeremiah 7:22–23) (Zechariah 7:10) (Mark 11:25) (1 Timothy 2:8–10).

title: Conditions of true prayer from Scripture

english: This was said hypothetically — even if nothing else attends us praying — that we gain the best, conceiving and achieving the 'how' of prayer. But clearly one who so prays shall be heard even while speaking, beholding by the Hearer's activity 'Behold, I am here,' having shed before praying all displeasure toward providence. For this is declared by: If you remove from yourself bond and finger-pointing and murmuring word — of one well-pleased with what happens, free from every bond, not voting against God who ordains what he wills for our training, nor murmuring in the hidden reasonings without audible voice to men — which murmuring, like wicked servants who blame masters' (Isaiah 58:9) orders, murmur those who dare not with voice and whole soul curse providence for what happens, yet wish to escape the Lord of all in what displeases them. And I think this is also the Job passage: In all these things that happened Job sinned not with his lips before God. On the earlier-recorded temptation: In all these things that happened Job sinned not before God. Which, commanding it must not happen, the word in Deuteronomy says: Take heed lest there be a hidden word in your heart, lawlessness, saying: The seventh year draws near — and what follows.

One who so prays, so greatly profited beforehand, becomes fitter to be mingled with the Spirit filling the whole world of the Lord and with him who filled all earth and heaven, saying through the prophet thus: Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord. Still, through the aforesaid purity and prayer, with the Word of God standing amid those encircling(?) him, nothing lacking to prayer, he shall partake — with him who is mediated by him(?) co-praying to the Father. For High Priest of our offerings and Paraclete to the Father is the Son of God, praying for those who pray and co-advocating with advocates — who would not pray for his own who do not pray more constantly through him, nor be Paraclete before God for those disobeying the teachings to pray always and not faint. For he spoke, it says, a parable to the effect that they must always pray and not faint: There was a judge in a certain city — and what follows. And before these: And he said to them: Which of you shall have a friend, and go to him at midnight and say to him: Friend, lend me three loaves, since a friend arrived to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him — and a little later: I say to you, though he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his shamelessness he will rise and give him whatever he needs. Who of those believing Jesus' unlying mouth would not be urged to pray untiringly, when he says: Ask, and it shall be given you — for everyone who asks receives? Since the good Father gives the living bread to us who ask him for it (not the stone the Adversary wants to become food for Jesus and his disciples), to those who received the spirit of adoption from the Father; and the Father gives the good gift, raining(?) it from heaven, to those who ask him (Isaiah 58:6) (Job 1:22) (Job 2:10) (Deuteronomy 15:9) (Jeremiah 23:24) (Luke 18:1) (Luke 11:5–8) (Matthew 7:7–8) (Matthew 4:3) (Romans 8:15) (Luke 11:13) (Job 1:22; 2:10) (Luke 18:1; 11:5–8).

title: Already gaining the how of prayer

english: Not only the High Priest co-prays with the genuine prayers, but also the angels rejoicing in heaven — over one sinner repenting or over ninety-nine righteous needing no repentance — and the souls of the departed saints. This is shown when Raphael offers rational worship to God for Tobit and Sarah (for after both prayed: 'Heard,' says Scripture, 'was the prayer of both before the glory of the great Raphael, and he was sent to heal the two.' (Luke 15:7) And Raphael himself, revealing his angelic commission to both by God's command, says: 'And now, when you prayed, you and Sarah your bride, I brought the memorial of your prayer before the Holy One.' (Luke 15:10) And a little later: 'I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who bring up the prayers of the saints and enter before the glory of the Holy One' (Tobit 12:8)). At any rate Raphael's word: 'Prayer with fasting and alms and righteousness is good.' (Tobit 12:12) And Jeremiah — appearing in Maccabees, eminent in gray hair and glory, so that his eminence was something marvelous and most magnificent, holding out his right hand and giving Judas a golden sword — another departed saint bore witness, saying: 'This is he who prays much for the people and the holy city, Jeremiah, God's prophet.'

It would be absurd — with knowledge now manifest to the worthy through a mirror, in an enigma, but then revealed face to face — not to conceive the analogy for the remaining virtues, perfected then properly in those prepared in this life. One chiefest virtue by the divine word is love of neighbor — which we must conceive present far more in departed saints toward life's strugglers than among those in human weakness co-struggling with inferiors: not only here, where 'if one member suffers, all members suffer with it; if one member is glorified, all members rejoice with it' (Tobit 12:15) holds among brother-lovers. Fitting too for love beyond this life to say: 'The care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is stumbled, and I do not burn?' (2 Maccabees 15:12–16) And this, with Christ confessing that like each ailing saint he likewise ails, is in prison, goes naked and abroad, hungers and thirsts. Who reading the Gospel does not know Christ reckoning what befalls believers, by reference to himself, as his own sufferings?

If God's angels came to Jesus and ministered to him — and it is not fitting to conceive the angels' ministry to Jesus as lasting a short time of his bodily sojourn among men, with him still amid believers not as reclining but as ministering — how many angels, likely, minister to Jesus, who wants to gather Jerusalem's children one by one(?) and collect the diaspora, saving God-fearers and callers, co-working the church's growth and multitude more than the apostles: as some angels presiding over churches are named by John in Revelation? For not in vain do God's angels ascend and descend upon the Son of Man, seen by eyes lit with gnosis's light.

At prayer-time itself, then, reminded by the pray-er of what he needs, they do what they can, having received it as universal command. Use some such image for this discourse, to admit what we conceived: suppose a physician of righteousness, caring for a sick pray-er about health, knowing how one must heal the disease so-and-so's prayer reports. Evidently he will be moved to heal the pray-er — supposing, not idly, that this very thing came into God's mind, who heard the prayer of one who prayed for release from disease. Or one of the rich in life's needs in excess, [sharing?] ... interceding with God — evidently he too will fulfill prayer's [petitions?] to the [asker]. [Rough tail.] As servant becoming of the father's counsel who brought together at prayer-time the giver with the pray-er — since rightness(?) of choice cannot overlook the asker of these things.

As these must not be thought to happen by chance, when they happen — with the counter of all the saints' head-hairs harmoniously bringing together at prayer-time the future servant-benefactor, hearing, to the faithful asker — so we must suppose angels overseeing and ministering to God sometimes gather in presence to some pray-er, to breathe with what he asked. And each one's angel — even of the church's little ones(?) — ever beholding the face of the Father in heaven and beholding our Creator's divinity, co-prays with us and co-works, where possible, in what we pray (1 Corinthians 13:12) (1 Corinthians 12:26) (2 Corinthians 11:28–29) (Matthew 25:35–36) (Matthew 23:37) (John 1:51) (Matthew 10:30) (Matthew 18:10) (Luke 15:7,10) (Tobit 12:8,12,15).

title: Christ, angels, and the saints pray with us

english: Besides, I hold the words of the saints' prayer full of power — especially when praying they pray in spirit and with the mind: like light dawning from the pray-er's thought and proceeding from his mouth, by God's power dissolving the intelligible poison shot by opposing powers at the ruling part of those neglecting to pray and not keeping Paul's 'pray unceasingly,' spoken after Jesus' exhortations. For like an arrow from the pray-er's soul, with knowledge and word or faith, it goes forth from the holy one, wounding unto destruction the spirits hostile to God, who want to cast us into sin's bonds.

One prays unceasingly when works of virtue, or commandments performed, are taken up as part of prayer — joining prayer to needful works and befitting deeds to prayer. Only thus can we receive 'pray unceasingly' as possibly spoken: if we call the saint's whole life one continuous great prayer, of which the customarily-named prayer is part, owed no less than thrice daily — clear from Daniel, praying thrice a day with such danger hanging over him. And Peter going up to the roof to pray at the sixth hour, when he saw the vessel coming down from heaven let down by four corners, exhibits the middle of the three prayers: with before it the one spoken by David, 'In the morning You shall hear my prayer; in the morning I shall present myself to You and watch' (1 Corinthians 14:15); and the last shown by 'The lifting of my hands, an evening sacrifice.' (1 Thessalonians 5:17) Nor should we duly pass the night season without this prayer — with David saying, 'At midnight I rose to confess to You for Your righteous judgments,' (Daniel 6:10) and Paul, as Acts says, at midnight with Silas in Philippi praying and hymning God, so that even the prisoners overheard them (Acts 10:9) (Acts 10:11) (Psalm 5:4) (Psalm 141:2) (Psalm 119:62) (Acts 16:25) (Acts 10:9–11) (Psalm 5:4; 141:2; 119:62).

The 'one continuous great prayer' (whole virtuous life) with thrice-daily customary prayer inside it is Origen's solution to 1 Thess 5:17; Daniel/Peter/David/Paul-Silas are the proof.
title: Power in the prayers of the saints

english: If Jesus prays, and prays not in vain — obtaining what he asks through praying, which perhaps he would not have received without prayer — who of us neglects praying? Mark says: 'Rising very early in the night he went out and departed to a desert place, and there prayed.' (Mark 1:35) Luke: 'And it came to pass, as he was praying in a certain place' (Luke 11:1) — and elsewhere: 'And he spent the night in the prayer of God.' (Luke 6:12) John records his prayer, saying: 'These things Jesus spoke, and lifting his eyes to heaven he said: Father, the hour has come; glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You.' (John 17:1) And 'I knew that You always hear me,' (Esther 4:16) recorded by him as spoken by the Lord, shows that always praying he is always heard.

Why list those benefited by God for praying in the 'what' manner, heard obtaining what they prayed? Hannah, believing though barren to pray — whereby she was wholly deemed worthy to bear Samuel the prophet, numbered after Moses. And Hezekiah, childless, learning from Isaiah he would die, achieving by prayer to be numbered among my Savior's forefathers. The Mordecai and Esther matters — heard through prayer and fasting, Jews feast the feast of salvation to this day on Mordecai's joyful narratives, a Mordecai-day beside Moses'. The Judith matters — achieving with God by holy prayer against Holofernes, one Hebrew woman shamed Nebuchadnezzar the Assyrian king's house. The Ananias, Azarias, Misael matters — praying, a fine breeze of dew breathing on the furnace flame, deeming them worthy not to smell fire. The Daniel matters — the lions muzzled for Daniel's prayers. And Jonah too, not despairing of being heard from the swallower's belly, coming out of the fish's belly fills the lack of the Ninevites prophecy.

What things each of us has — if thankfully mindful of benefits passed over him he confesses — now to bless the Lord, to glorify His name! That our barren and sterile souls, through prayer's continuance bearing saving words, got children from them? That enemies dissolved — though myriads of hostile power often camped against us, wanting to wipe us from divine faith? Did not, as David said, 'these in chariots and these in horses, but we shall be magnified in the Lord our God's name? They were hamstrung and fell, but we rose and stood upright?' And again, as written: 'A horse is false for salvation, nor shall he be saved by his power's multitude?' And the opposing commander with his plausible deceiving word cut down through the God hymned and glorified in us — and Judith herself, that is, confession (for Judith means confession), awaiting growth and fruits through God's wonder-worthy virtue? And that in trials fire touched us not, nor was fire's smell in us? And the lions' mouths muzzled, unable to make Christ's members food? And fleeing death through repentance we were saved, not despairing of being heard even in death's very belly? For death having prevailed swallowed, and again God wiped every tear from every face.

These seem to me most necessary, after the catalogue of prayer's beneficiaries, for spiritual-life lovers: that in the present season we pray not about small earthly things, but are led up to mystic things, using these expounded ones as types. Willing to follow anagoge with the letter rather than bare history, to train ourselves not barren nor sterile of words, hearing spiritual law with spiritual ears — to be heard as Hannah and Hezekiah; to be saved from intelligible enemies as Mordecai, Esther, Judith; with Egypt the iron furnace, the earthly place (a symbol, then, being fired in Egypt [?]), no less to thank, escaping it, than those tested in furnace fire kept unwet(?) safe; 'deliver not to beasts a soul confessing to You' (John 11:42) to be heard; kept unharmed of asp and basilisk, to hymn and thank our Rescuer from them.

Nor shall Jonah's type be idle for the willing examiner — who, reading the fish-belly records and hearing Job say 'cursed be that day,' will tame the great sea-beast — himself beginning no more to resist but obediently to obey [rough]: repenting in the fish's belly, coming out to persist in obedience and prophesy salvation to perishing Ninevites, neither begrudging God's kindness nor demanding severity to penitents. Nor is Samuel's greatest work through prayer's spirit spiritually possible for each genuinely God-devoted now worthy to be heard: 'Stand and see this great word the Lord will do before your eyes. Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call the Lord, and he will give voices and rain.' (1 Samuel 1:20) And Samuel called to the Lord, and the Lord gave voices and rain that day. Every saint genuinely discipled by Jesus hears: 'Lift your eyes and see the fields, white to harvest already; the reaper receives wage and gathers fruit to eternal life.' (2 Kings 20:1–6) For in harvest season the Lord does a great word before prophets' hearers: when the Spirit-adorned calls to the Lord, God gives voices and soul-watering rain — that the formerly evil, fearing the Lord and God's benefaction's minister, reverend and venerable toward penitents as manifested. And Elijah, after heaven shut to the godless three years and six months, opens it later by divine word — which is achieved by everyone receiving soul-rain through prayer, previously deprived of it (Judith 13:8) (Daniel 3:27) (Daniel 6:22) (Jonah 2:1–10) (Psalm 20:7) (Psalm 33:17) (Isaiah 25:8) (Deuteronomy 4:20) (Psalm 74:19) (Psalm 91:13) (Job 3:3) (1 Samuel 12:16–18) (John 4:35–36) (James 5:17) (Mark 1:35; Luke 11:1; 6:12; John 17:1; 11:42) (Psalm 20:7; 33:17; Isaiah 25:8) (Psalm 74:19; 91:13) (1 Samuel 12:16–18; John 4:35–36; James 5:17).

title: Jesus himself prayed — and was heard

english: With these benefits to holy men through prayers expounded as we could, let us examine, from the Gospel record 'Ask for the great things, and the small shall be added to you; and ask for the heavenly things, and the earthly shall be added to you,' (Matthew 6:8) what asking great heavenly things is, and small earthly things. For that all visibles are symbols and types, since intelligibles are true — a worthy argument will persuade one hastening from visibles and phenomena alone to know intelligibles and invisibles, saying how the invisible God is seen through his works [rough]. And as dwelling among the notable advances taking on some character, so converse with saints through prayer is always useful toward imitating them — always both having prayed and been heard — and truly asking the same things they typically(?) asked: heavenly and great, shown through small earthly matters — that whoever wants to be spiritual, asking through prayers for heavenly great things, may inherit heaven's kingdom as heavenly and enjoy great goods as great — with earthly small things supplied to him by need's measure for bodily needs, since the Father knows what we need before we ask him.

Since with the apostle four names seem said for four things — 'I exhort then first of all that petitions, prayers, intercessions, thanksgivings be made for all men' (1 Timothy 2:1) — it is very useful for us to expound each separately as we can, what each signifies. Petition, then, we take to be some asking of a needy one for things he lacks. Prayer, a nobler asking with doxology for greater things. Intercession, a bolder asking to God from one having more frankness. Thanksgiving, confession with prayer for benefits received — or for the magnitude of benefits, appearing great to the benefited.

Take examples of the first: 'Fear not, Zechariah,' (Matthew 17:15) says Gabriel, 'for your petition was heard; Elizabeth your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.' (Luke 1:13) And Moses making petition for the calf-sinners: 'Why rage with anger, Lord, against Your people?' (Exodus 32:11) [rough bridge: since forgiving this sin was grave, with fasts and after them reporting petition for them to God from himself at once: 'forty days and forty nights bread was not eaten nor water drunk.' (Deuteronomy 9:18)] And Mordecai saying: 'And now, remembering all the works...' (Esther 4:17) and made petition with fasting and strong cry to the Lord, saying: 'Lord, Lord, King Almighty ...' (Matthew 11:25) And Esther herself says: 'And now ... of the Lord God of Israel' (Daniel 3:26) and said: 'Lord, our King —' [fragments].

Of the second take such examples: Azariah standing and praying these words amid fire, saying: 'Blessed are You, Lord God of our fathers; praised and glorified Your name forever; we were not shamed ...' (Tobit 3:1–2) And Tobit in weeping remembering God: 'I prayed with pain and said: Righteous are You, Lord, and all Your works and all Your ways mercy and truth; You judge true and righteous judgment forever ...' (Habakkuk 3:1–2) How and in what way Daniel prayed we do not know, since Daniel's Song was obelized from the Hebrew — this at least we know by their view: by the circumcision-party Tobit and Judith are not at all received, as not even written in the covenant(?) [rough]. Hence we shall have Habakkuk's and Hannah's examples, with no other such words anywhere in their prayers: 'A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet with song: Lord, I heard Your hearing and feared; I considered Your works and was amazed. Amid two lives You shall be known; as years draw near You shall be recognized; when the season comes You shall be shown.' (Jonah 2:2–4) And Jonah's: 'Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the fish's belly and said: I cried in my affliction to the Lord my God, and he heard me; from Hades' belly You heard my cry's voice. You cast me into sea-heart depths' — and what follows.

Of the third we shall have examples — intercession: with prayer being for us, and the Spirit making intercession. It is something better and bolder than the one for whom it intercedes: 'What to pray as we ought we know not, but the Spirit itself intercedes with unutterable groanings.' (Romans 8:26–27) For the Spirit intercedes and entreats(?), while we pray. And Joshua son of Nun — he said to the Lord in the day the Lord delivered the Amorite before Israel, when he crushed them at Gibeon and pursued them, and said: 'Let the sun stand over Gibeon and the moon over Aijalon valley.' (Joshua 10:12–13) Even if Scripture, not saying 'intercession' but saying 'he said,' hearing such is intercession — if we hear names more strictly. And Samson saying, 'Let my soul die with the foreigners,' (Judges 16:30) makes intercession; for he died with the house falling on him and the foreigners.

Petition, intercession, thanksgiving must be made not only to God but also to holy men: Paul and Peter, to benefit us and make us worthy of their forgiveness of sins; and to one not happening to be a saint, but against whom wrongdoers seek pardon, one must petition and intercede. Much more both thank and intercede to Christ: Stephen says, 'Lord, lay not this sin to them.' (Luke 1:13; Exodus 32:11; Deuteronomy 9:18; Esther) The epileptic's father: 'I beg, Lord, have mercy' (Daniel 3:26; Tobit 3:1–2; Habakkuk 3:1–2; Jonah 2:2–4) — the son, or myself, or whomsoever. And the Lord's own voice we shall use as example, saying: 'I confess to You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth' (Acts 7:60) — with 'I confess' signifying 'I thank.' (Romans 8:26–27; Joshua 10:12–13; Judges 16:30) (Acts 7:60; Matthew 17:15; 11:25)

title: Ask for the great and heavenly things

english: If we hear what prayer is, perhaps no generated being at all is to be prayed to — not even Christ himself — but only the God of all and Father, to whom our Savior himself prayed, as we set out above, and teaches us to pray. For when he heard 'Teach us to pray,' he does not teach to pray to himself, but to the Father, saying 'Our Father who art in the heavens,' and what follows. For if the Son is other than the Father, as is shown elsewhere, in essence and in substrate — then either the Son is to be prayed to and not the Father, or both, or the Father alone. That the Son be prayed to and not the Father, anyone at all will agree is most absurd, said in the face of the plain evidence. But if both, then clearly we would address plural demands through our prayers, saying 'Grant, and do good, and supply, and save,' (Psalm 110:4) and anything like these — which is self-evidently unseemly, and no one can show it lying anywhere in the Scriptures, said by anyone. It remains, then, to pray to the God and Father of all alone — but not apart from the High Priest, who was established by the Father with an oath, according to 'He swore, and will not repent: thou art a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.' (Luke 11:1–2)

So when the saints give thanks in their prayers, they confess their thanks to God through Christ Jesus. And as the one who is exact about praying must not pray to the one who prays, but to him whom our Lord Jesus taught us to call Father over our prayers — so no prayer at all is to be offered to the Father apart from him, as he himself shows this plainly, saying: 'Amen, amen, I say to you: whatever you ask my Father, he will give you in my name. Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.' (John 16:23–24) For he did not say 'Ask me,' nor simply 'Ask the Father,' but: 'If you ask the Father, he will give you in my name.' (Deuteronomy 32:43) For until Jesus taught these things, no one had asked the Father in the name of the Son — and true was the saying, spoken by Jesus, 'Until now you have asked nothing in my name,' (Isaiah 49:22–23) and true also is 'Ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.' (Mark 10:18)

But if someone, supposing that Christ himself must be prayed to, confuses the issue and brings against us, from what worship signifies, the 'Let all the angels of God worship him' (Hebrews 4:15) — spoken of Christ, as all agree, in Deuteronomy — we must say to him that Jerusalem too, the church, named by the prophet, is said to be worshiped by kings and rulers, who become her nurses and nourishers, in these words: 'Behold, I lift my hand to the nations, and to the islands I will raise my signal, and they shall bring thy sons in the bosom, and carry thy daughters on shoulders; and kings shall be thy nurses, and their princesses thy nourishers; they shall worship thee on the face of the earth, and lick the dust of thy feet. And thou shalt know that I am the Lord, and shalt not be ashamed.' (Galatians 4:5–6)

And how is it not in keeping with the one who said, 'Why callest thou me good? None is good but one, God, the Father,' (Psalm 22:23) to say: 'Why pray to me? To the Father alone must you pray — to whom I too pray'? Which you learn through the holy Scriptures. For you must not pray to the High Priest established for you by the Father, who has received from the Father to be a Paraclete — but through the High Priest and Paraclete, who can sympathize with your weaknesses, having been tempted in all things as you are, yet, by the gift of the Father to me, tempted apart from sin. Learn, then, what a gift you have received from my Father, having received by the new birth in me the spirit of adoption, that you may be called sons of God, and my brothers. For you have read the voice spoken through David by me concerning you to the Father: 'I will declare thy name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will sing to thee.' But for those counted worthy of one Father with them to pray to a brother is not reasonable; to the Father alone, with me and through me, must prayer be sent up by you.

title: Pray to the Father, not to any creature

english: When we hear Jesus saying these things, then, let us pray to God through him, all saying the same thing, not even split over the manner of prayer. Or are we not split, if some of us pray to the Father and others to the Son — erring a layman's error, held with great integrity but untested and unexamined, when those who pray to the Son, whether with the Father or apart from the Father, go wrong? Let us pray to God; let us address with entreaty as to a Father; let us make petition as of a Lord; let us give thanks as to God and Father and Lord — to one who is not Lord of a slave without qualification. For 'Father' may reasonably be taken as Lord both of the Son and, through him, of the sons who have become sons; and as there is no God of the dead but of the living, so there is no Lord of unborn slaves, but of those who at first are nobly nurtured by fear, because of infancy, and afterwards serve the more blessed service in love rather than the service in fear. For there are also in the soul, to him alone who sees the heart, manifest characters of God's slaves and of his sons.

Everyone, then, who asks earthly and small things of God disobeys the one who commanded to ask heavenly and great things of the God who knows how to grant nothing earthly or small. But if someone brings up against this the things granted to the saints in answer to prayer concerning the body — and even the voice of the Gospel, which teaches that earthly and small things are also added to us — we must answer him that, just as, when someone grants us a body of some sort, we must not say that so-and-so granted us the shadow of the body (for he did not give the body with the purpose of granting two things, body and shadow; the purpose of the giver is to give a body, and receiving its shadow follows upon the gift of the body) — so, if with our mind grown nobler we were to contemplate the gifts principally given us by God, we shall most fittingly call the bodily things concomitants of the great and heavenly spiritual graces, given to each of the saints for his profit, whether according to the analogy of faith or as the giver wills — and he wills wisely, even if we cannot state for each gift a cause and a reason worthy of the giver. [At this point the margin of the chief manuscript is damaged for about five lines; the editors leave the gap unfilled.]

The soul of Hannah, then, changed from a kind of barrenness, had borne fruit more than her body, which conceived Samuel; and Hezekiah had more divinely begotten children of mind than of body, though they were born of his bodily seed. [Here the chief manuscript is corrupt, with a marginal note that the text has failed; the sense concerns Esther and Mordecai and the people profiting more from intelligible deliverance than from Haman and his fellow-conspirators, who wished to destroy them.] Or who was mocked(?) — even that Holofernes? But the invisible lions were muzzled to the prophet Daniel, unable to act against his soul, rather than the visible ones — concerning whom all who meet with Scripture itself have learned. And what of the bodily dew, which overcame the flame of Nebuchadnezzar — did it come to be more than the spiritual dew? And who so escaped the belly of the sea-monster, tamed under Jesus our Savior, which swallows every fugitive from God, as Jonah, becoming capable of the holy things of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 22:32) (1 Corinthians 12:7) (Romans 12:6) (1 Corinthians 12:11)?

title: One prayer to God through Christ

english: It is no wonder that, just as not the same shadow is given to all who receive, so to speak, the bodies that make such shadows — to some no shadow at all, to others the same shadow — so too with the prior gifts. For this is plainly seen to hold for bodies as well by those who study gnomonic problems and the ratio of shadows to the illuminating body: for gnomons are shadowless at certain seasons, and others have, so to speak, short shadows, and others longer shadows than others. It is no great thing, then, if — since the purpose of the giver who grants the prior gifts fits them by certain ineffable and mystical analogies to the receivers and to the times when the prior gifts are given — at one time no shadows at all follow the receivers, at another not all but few, at another lesser ones by comparison, with greater ones following others. As, then, one who seeks the sun's rays is neither gladdened nor grieved by the presence or absence of the bodies' shadow, having the most necessary thing — whether enlightened or deprived of the shadow, or having more or less of the shadow — so, if the spiritual gifts are with us and we are enlightened by God toward the complete possession of the true goods, we shall not fuss over a cheap matter of shadow. For all material and bodily things, whatever they may be, have the worth of a faint and feeble shadow, wholly unable to be compared with the saving and holy gifts of the God of all. For what comparison is there of bodily wealth with the wealth 'in all speech' and 'all' wisdom?

And who but a madman would compare health of flesh and bones with a healthy and vigorous soul and well-measured reasonings? All of which, ordered by the word of God, make bodily sufferings some cheap scratch — even if we count the scratch briefer than it is. But he who has contemplated what the beauty of the bride is, whose 'songs' the word of God loves — a soul in bloom with supercelestial and supermundane beauty — will be ashamed to honor with the same name of beauty the bodily beauty of woman or boy or ... Flesh is as grass, and its 'glory,' which appears in what is called the beauty of women and children, has been likened by the prophetic word to a flower, saying: 'All flesh is as grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass is withered, and the flower fallen; but the word of the Lord abides forever.' (1 Corinthians 1:5) But who will properly call nobility the trite thing called so among men, who has conceived the nobility of sons of God? And the mind that has contemplated Christ's 'unshakable' kingdom — how will it not despise as worth nothing 'all the kingdom upon earth' (Isaiah 40:6–8)? And having seen, as far as a human mind still bound in body can hold, and grasped as far as possible, the army of angels and archistrategi — among them powers of the Lord, archangels and thrones and dominions and principalities and authorities, supercelestial — how will it not, even if feebler than a shadow, despise as dimmest, comparing them, even these things admired among the senseless as worth no account, even if all these are given — and overlook them all, for the sake of not missing the true principalities and the more divine authorities? We must pray, then, pray concerning the prior and truly great and heavenly things, and leave the matters of the shadows that follow the prior things to God, who knows 'what need' we have, through the mortal body, 'before' we ask him (Hebrews 12:28) (Colossians 1:16 (thrones) (Matthew 6:8) (Colossians 1:16).

title: Different measures of spiritual gifts

english: Now in these matters, sufficiently — according to the grace given, as far as we have been enabled — by God through his Christ (would that it were also in the Holy Spirit; whether this is so, judge as you meet with what we have said in Scripture, examining the problem concerning the soul), we shall now come to the next contest also, wishing to contemplate with what power the prayer outlined by the Lord is filled.

And first of all it must be observed that Matthew and Luke might seem to most to have recorded the same prayer outlined for how we must pray. But the words of Matthew run in this way: 'Our Father who art in the heavens, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done, as in heaven, also upon earth; give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors; and bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.' (Matthew 6:9–13) And those of Luke: 'Father, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; our daily bread give us day by day; and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us; and bring us not into temptation.' (Luke 11:2–4)

But we must say to those who suppose so, first, that the phrases, though neighboring one another in some things, are plainly seen to differ in others, as we shall show when we examine them; and second, that it is impossible for the same prayer to have been spoken both on the mountain — where, seeing the crowds, he went up, and when he had sat down his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught (for it stands recorded with Matthew in the sequence of the announcement concerning the beatitudes and the commandments that follow) — and 'when he was in a certain place' (Matthew 5:1–2) praying, 'when he ceased,' spoken to one of the disciples who asked to be taught — presumably not present then, when he spoke the words in Matthew, or not retaining what had long ago been said. Or perhaps it is better to consider the prayers different, having some parts in common. And though we searched Mark as well, lest any equivalent recorded prayer escape us, we found not even a trace of a prayer lying there (Luke 11:1).
