title: Enough said — toward the Lord’s Prayer

english: Since, as we said in what went before, the one who prays must first be established — how disposed and in what condition — and only then pray, let us see, before the prayer that lies in Matthew, the words spoken about it by our Savior, which run thus: 'When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites; for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward. But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and shut thy door, and pray to thy Father who is in secret; and thy Father who sees in secret shall repay thee. And when you pray, do not babble as the heathen do; for they think that in their much speaking they shall be heard. Be not like them, then; for your Father knows what need you have before you ask him. Pray, then, like this.' (Matthew 6:5–9)

In many places, then, our Savior is seen pressing against ambition as a passion that destroys; which he has done here also, turning men away from performing a hypocrite's work at the season of prayer. For it is a hypocrite's work to want to preen oneself before men for piety or for fellowship. But we must remember the 'How can you believe, who receive glory from men, and seek not the glory that comes from the only God?' (John 5:44) — and despise all glory from men, even if it is thought to come of the good — and seek the sovereign and true glory, the glory from the only God, who becomingly glorifies, beyond the worth of the glorified, the one worthy of glory. Even what was thought good and praiseworthy is polluted when deemed to be done — when we do it 'that we may be glorified by men' or 'that we may be seen by men.' That is why no recompense from God follows upon it. For every word of Jesus is unlying — and, if one must force the saying, becomes more unlying still when spoken with his customary oath. He says of those who do good for show to win human glory, or who pray 'in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets' (Luke 16:25) 'that they may be seen by men,' the same thing: 'Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward.' (Galatians 6:8) For as the rich man in Luke 'received his good things' in his human 'life' — and, having drawn them off, has no more room to receive them after this present life — so he who draws off 'his reward' for himself, whether in giving to someone or in prayers, as one who sowed 'not to the Spirit' but 'to the flesh,' shall 'reap corruption' indeed, but shall not 'reap eternal life.' He sows 'to the flesh' who, 'in the synagogues and in the streets, that' (Matthew 6:2) he may be glorified 'by men,' gives 'alms' with a trumpet 'before' himself, or who, loving 'to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets, that,' (Matthew 7:13) having been seen 'by men,' he may be reputed by the onlookers to be some pious and holy man.

But everyone who walks the broad and roomy way that leads away 'to destruction' — which has nothing straight or direct, but is all crooked and cornered (for it is rent by 'corners,' in which 'men' who, dying because they have fallen from divinity, 'glorify and bless' those reputed among them to be impious in the streets) — and many there always are who appear in prayer to be lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, getting drunk on prayer in the midst of banquets and beside wine, truly 'standing on the corners of the streets' and praying. For everyone who lives for pleasure, loving the roomy way, has fallen out of the narrow and straitened way of Jesus Christ, which has not even a chance bend, and is nowhere at all cornered.
translator_notes: 'Pressing against ambition as a passion that destroys' — φιλοδοξία as ὀλέθριον πάθος; kept clinical.
'More unlying still' renders the forced oxymoron ἀψευδέστερος (truth beyond truth under oath).
'Rent by corners' (κέκλασται ... γεγωνιωμένην): the broad way is broken into street-corners — the geometry of show.
title: How one must be disposed before praying

english: But there is a difference between church and synagogue: the church, properly speaking, 'has no spot or wrinkle or any such thing,' (Ephesians 5:27) but is holy and blameless — into which neither one 'born of a harlot' enters, nor the 'crushed' or 'cut off,' nor an Egyptian or Idumaean, unless, with sons born to them, they can barely be fitted to the church by the third generation, nor a Moabite or Ammonite, unless a tenth generation be fulfilled and an age completed; while the synagogue is built by a centurion — he did this in the times before the sojourn of Jesus, when faith had not yet been witnessed, such 'as not even in Israel' (Colossians 2:3) did the Son of God find. He, then, who loves 'to pray' 'in the synagogues' is not far from the corners 'of the streets.' But the saint is not like that: for he does not love 'to pray' but loves it, and not 'in synagogues' but in churches, and not 'on corners of streets' (John 14:23) but in the straightness of the narrow and straitened way — and not 'that he may be seen by men' but that he may be seen 'before the Lord God.' For it is a male thing to know 'the acceptable year of the Lord' and to keep the commandment that says: 'Three times in the year shall every male appear before the Lord God.' (Deuteronomy 23:1–4)

But the 'that they may be seen' must be heard exactly: nothing seen is good — as if it were by seeming, and did not truly stamp the impression, misleading it instead of impressing it exactly and truly. As the actors of certain dramas in the theaters are not what they say, nor, in respect of the mask they wear, are they what they are seen to be — so all who mold the impression of the good by seeming are not righteous but hypocrites of righteousness, acting their hypocrisy in their own theater, 'in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets.' (Luke 7:5) But he who is no hypocrite, stripping off everything foreign, and furnishing himself to please, in a theater incomparably greater than all the theater aforesaid — enters into his own 'closet,' shutting upon the stored wealth the treasure 'of wisdom and knowledge' for himself; and nodding nowhere outward, gaping after nothing outward, shutting every 'door' of the senses, lest he be dragged by the senses and their impression steal in upon his mind — prays to the Father who neither flees nor forsakes such secrecy but dwells in it, with the Only-begotten present with him. For 'I,' he says, 'and the Father will come to him and make our abode with him.' (Exodus 23:17) And it is plain that the righteous, if we so pray, shall address not God only but a Father — as sons not left behind, with him present in our 'secret,' watching it and doing more things in the storehouse, if we shut 'its door.'
translator_notes: 'Does not love to pray but loves it' (οὐ φιλεῖ ... ἀλλὰ ἀγαπᾷ): philein/loving vs agapan/loving — the saint's love is agape, not fondness.
'A male thing' (ἄῤῥην): manliness as spiritual maturity before the Lord; kept literal with the Ex 23:17 ground.
'Characters' implied: hypocrite as ὑποκριτής (mask-actor) — theater vocabulary kept throughout.
title: Church and synagogue

english: When praying, then, let us not babble but theologize. We babble when, without blaming ourselves or the words of prayer we send up, we speak corrupt works or words or thoughts — lowly and blameworthy things, foreign to the Lord's incorruption. The babbler in his praying is already in a worse and harsher synagogue-condition than those named before — in a way worse than the corners in the streets — preserving not even a trace of the hypocrisy of the good. For, according to the word of the Gospel, only 'the heathen babble,' who have not even an impression of great or heavenly petitions, sending up every prayer about bodily and outward things. The one who asks lowly things of the Lord who dwells in heaven and above the heights of the heavens is likened to a babbling heathen.

And the wordy seems to babble, and the babbler to be wordy. For nothing of matter and bodies is one: each thing deemed one is split and hewn apart and divided into many, having lost unity. For the good is one, but base things are many; and truth is one, but falsehoods are many; and true righteousness is one, but many are the conditions that play the hypocrite toward it; and the wisdom of God is one, but many are the wisdoms 'of this age' and 'of the rulers of this age' (Matthew 6:7) that are being brought to nought; and the Word of God is one, but many are the words foreign to God. That is why no one shall escape 'sin' 'from wordiness,' and no one who thinks to be heard 'from wordiness' can be heard. So our prayers must not be likened to heathen who babble or are wordy or do whatever they do 'after the likeness of the serpent.' (1 Corinthians 2:6) For the God of the saints 'knows' 'before' what things his sons 'have need of,' since they are worthy of the Father's knowledge. But if anyone does not know God, he does not know the things of God either — and he does not know 'what need' he has: for the things he thinks he needs are wide of the mark. But he who has contemplated what better and more divine things he lacks, known by God, shall obtain what he contemplated, known to the Father even before the asking. So much, then, for what is said before the prayer in Matthew; now let us contemplate also what is declared by the prayer (Proverbs 10:19) (Matthew 6:8).
notes_covered: Wordiness multiplies; the One vs the many
translator_notes: 'Theologize' (θεολογήσωμεν) set against 'babble' (βαττολογήσωμεν): wordplay kept as coined pair.
'The One vs the many' — Origen's metaphysics of unity (good/truth/righteousness/wisdom/Word, each one) against material multiplicity.
'After the likeness of the serpent': the babbler's hiss — πολλὰ ... wordiness as serpentine.
title: Do not babble — speak of God

english: 'Our Father who art in the heavens.' (Philippians 3:20) It is worth watching more exactly whether the old covenant, as it is called, has anywhere in it a prayer of someone calling God Father. For at present, examining as we can, we have not found one. We do not say this — that God has not been called Father, or that those deemed to have believed God have not been named sons of God — but that in prayer we have not yet found the frankness announced by the Savior concerning naming God Father. That God has been called Father, and that those who have come to the word of God are sons, can be seen in many places — as in Deuteronomy: 'Thou hast forsaken God who begot thee, and forgotten God who nourishes thee' (Deuteronomy 32:6,18,20); and again: 'Is not this thy Father who bought thee and made thee and created thee?' (Isaiah 1:2); and again: 'Sons, in whom there is no faith'; and in Isaiah: 'Sons I begot and raised, but they rejected me' (Malachi 1:6); and in Malachi: 'A son shall glorify his father, and a servant his master. And if I am a Father, where is my glory? And if I am a Master, where is my fear?' (Galatians 4:1–5)

If, then, God is called Father, and those begotten by the word of faith in him are sons, yet the firm and unfallen character of sonship is not to be seen among the ancients. At any rate the very passages we set out show those called sons to be blameworthy — since, according to the Apostle, 'while the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a slave, though lord of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the term appointed by the father.' (Romans 8:15–17) But 'the fullness of time' lies in the sojourn of our Lord Jesus Christ, when those who will receive the adoption — as Paul teaches in these words: 'For you received not a spirit of slavery unto fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, wherein we cry: Abba, Father.' (John 1:12) And in John: 'But as many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God — to those who believe in his name.' (1 John 3:8–9) And that is why, concerning those born of God, we have learned through the 'spirit of adoption' in John's catholic epistle that 'everyone born of God does no sin, for his seed abides in him' (1 Corinthians 12:3) — and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.

But if we consider what 'When you pray, say: Father' — as written with Luke — is, we shall hesitate, unless we have become genuine sons, to bring this voice to him — lest, besides our other sins, we become liable to a charge of impiety as well. What I say is like this. Paul says in First Corinthians: 'No one can say: Lord Jesus, except in the Holy Spirit; and no one speaking in the Spirit of God says: Anathema Jesus' (Romans 10:10) — naming the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of God as the same. But what saying 'in the Holy Spirit' 'Lord Jesus' is, is not at all plain — when myriads of hypocrites and still more heterodox utter the voice, and at times even demons, overcome by the power in the name. No one will dare to declare that any of these says 'Lord Jesus' 'in the Holy Spirit.' So they would not even be shown to say 'Lord Jesus' — only those who say it from their disposition, serving the word of God and proclaiming no other Lord in whatever they do: that is 'Lord Jesus.' And if such are those who say 'Lord Jesus,' then perhaps everyone who sins, outlawing the divine Word by transgression, cries out by his works: 'Anathema Jesus.' As, then, the one so disposed says 'Lord Jesus,' and the one oppositely disposed says 'Anathema Jesus' — so everyone 'born of God' 'and doing no sin,' by sharing God's seed, which turns him from all sin — by what he does he says 'Our Father who art in the heavens,' with his own spirit bearing witness with their spirit 'that they are children of God' — and his heirs, 'joint-heirs with Christ,' since suffering together they reasonably hope to be glorified together. And lest such say 'Our Father' only by halves, with their works their heart too — the fountain and source of good works — 'believes unto righteousness,' with which the mouth in agreement confesses 'unto salvation.'

Every work of theirs, then, and word and thought, formed by the Only-begotten Word after himself, has imitated the 'image of the invisible God' and become 'after the image of him who created' — who makes 'his sun rise' 'on evil and good' and sends rain 'on righteous and unrighteous' — so that 'the image of the heavenly' is in them, since he is the image of God. Being 'images,' then, of the Image — the Image being Son — the saints wipe off(?) sonship(?) — not only by becoming conformed in body to the body of Christ's glory, but also while being in 'the body.' And they become conformed to the One in the 'body of glory' by being 'transformed by the renewal of the mind.' (Colossians 1:15) But if such say 'Our Father who art in the heavens' in all things, then plainly 'he who does sin' — as John says in the catholic epistle — 'is of the devil, for the devil sins from the beginning.' (Matthew 5:45) And as God's 'seed,' abiding in the one 'born of God,' causes the inability to sin in the one formed after the Only-begotten Word — so in everyone who 'does sin' there is the devil's 'seed,' so far as it is present in the soul, not permitting its possessor to succeed. But since 'for this the Son of God was manifested, that he might loose the works of the devil,' (1 Corinthians 15:49) it is possible, by the visitation of God's Word upon our soul — the 'devil's' works being loosed — for the evil 'seed' implanted in us to be wiped away, and for us to become 'children of God.'

Let us not suppose, then, that we are taught to say phrases at some appointed season of praying. If we understood what was examined before about praying 'without ceasing,' our whole life — as of those who pray 'without ceasing' — should say 'Our Father who art in the heavens,' having our 'citizenship' in no way on earth but in every way 'in the heavens,' since we are thrones of God, because God's kingdom is founded in all who bear 'the image of the heavenly' and have therefore become heavenly.
notes_covered: Seed of God vs devil (1 Jn 3:8-9)
translator_notes: παρρησία ('frankness') — the Savior announces a new boldness: calling God Father IN prayer; kept as 'frankness.'
'Images of the Image' (εἰκὼν εἰκόνος): saints image the Son who is God's Image — Origen's chain kept exact.
ἀπομάττονται ('wipe off'?) is textually uncertain here; rendered plainly with flag.
title: “Our Father who art in the heavens”

english: But when the Father of the saints is said to be 'in the heavens,' we must not suppose him circumscribed by a bodily figure, dwelling 'in the heavens' — for God would then be found smaller than the heavens, contained by the heavens that contain him. We must be persuaded that all things are contained and held together by him, through the unspeakable power of his divinity. And generally the words, taken at the letter, which seem to the simpler to say that God is in a place, must be transferred becomingly to the great and spiritual conceptions concerning God — such as these in John: 'Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour was come, that he should pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end' (John 13:1,3; 14:23,28; 16:5); and after a little: 'knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and goes to God' (Philippians 2:7); and after other things: 'You have heard that I said to you: I go, and come to you. If you loved me, you would rejoice that I go to the Father' (John 20:17); and again after other things: 'But now I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me: Whither goest thou?' (Genesis 3:8–9) For if these are to be taken locally, then plainly so is 'Jesus answered and said to them: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him.' (Leviticus 26:12)

But these things do not happen with a local passage concerning the Father and the Son toward the one who loves Jesus' word — nor, therefore, are they to be taken locally. The Word of God, condescending to us — humbled, as befits his own worth, when he is among men — is said to pass 'from this world to the Father,' that we too may contemplate him perfected there, returning from the emptiness with us, which 'he emptied himself' of, to his own fullness. There we too, using him as guide, shall be filled and delivered from all emptiness. Let the Word of God, then, depart 'to him who sent' him, leaving the world, and journey 'to the Father.' And the word at the end of John's Gospel, 'Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father,' (Genesis 4:16) let us seek to understand more mystically — of the Son's ascent 'to the Father,' conceived by us with holy clarity in a manner worthier of God: an ascent which mind ascends rather than body.

This, I take it, I have examined together with 'Our Father who art in the heavens' — to remove the low conception of God from those who think he is locally 'in the heavens,' and not to let anyone say God is in a bodily place (for it follows from this that he is also a body) — which draws after it the most impious doctrines, supposing him divisible and material and corruptible. For every body is divisible and material and corruptible. Or let them tell us — not idly fanciful but claiming to grasp things plainly — how there can be another nature besides the material. And since, even before Christ's bodily sojourn, many writings seem to say God is in a bodily place, it seems to me not out of place to set out a few of those as well, to remove all entanglement from those who, through boorishness, enclose the God over all in a small and narrow place, so far as they can. And first in Genesis: Adam and Eve, he says, 'heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the evening; and Adam and his wife hid from the face of the Lord God among the trees of the garden.' (Psalm 123:1) We shall say to those who will not come to the treasuries of the letter, nor even knock at first on its 'door,' whether they can present the Lord God — who fills 'heaven and earth,' who, as they suppose, uses the more bodily 'heaven' as throne and 'the earth' as 'footstool of his feet' — as contained by a place so small by comparison with the whole heaven and earth that the paradise they suppose bodily is not filled by God, but is greater than him in size, so as to hold him walking, with a 'voice' heard from the base of his feet. Still more absurd, on their view, is Adam and Eve hiding, for shame at God over the transgression, 'from the face of God among the trees of the garden.' (Ecclesiastes 5:1) For it is not said that they merely wished to hide so — but that they really 'hid.' And how, on their view, does God inquire of Adam, saying: 'Where art thou?'

We have discussed these things at greater length, examining Genesis; but now, not to pass over so great a problem in utter silence, let us sufficiently recall the 'I will dwell in them and walk in them,' (Isaiah 66:1) said by God in Deuteronomy. For whatever his walk among the saints is, such too is the walk in Paradise — with God hiding, and everyone who sins fleeing his oversight and falling from frankness. For so too 'Cain went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Nod over against Eden.' (Wisdom 7:25) As, then, he dwells in the saints, so also in heaven — that is, in every saint and in Christ, in whom are all the saved as 'luminaries' and stars of heaven — or even because of the saints in heaven he dwells there, according to the saying 'To thee I lifted my eyes, who dwellest in heaven.' And the saying in Ecclesiastes, 'Hasten not to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven above, and thou upon earth below,' means to declare the distance from those in the body — of lowliness — to those lifted by profit and the word, the angels and holy powers, and Christ himself. For it is not absurd that he himself should properly be the throne of the Father — allegorically called heaven — and his church, called earth, should be 'the footstool of his feet.'

We have added, then, a few sayings even from the old covenant, deemed to present God in a place — to persuade the reader on every side, with the power given us, to hear divine Scripture more loftily and more spiritually whenever it seems to teach that God is in a place. And these things had to be examined together with 'Our Father who art in the heavens' — as withdrawing, so to speak, God's essence from all generated things. For the things with which God's essence does not commune(?) receive a certain glory and power of God — and, if I may so speak, an effluence of divinity comes to be in them.
translator_notes: 'Returning ... to his own fullness' (παλινδρομοῦντα εἰς τὸ ἴδιον πλήρωμα): kenosis reversed; we are emptied of emptiness.
'An ascent which mind ascends rather than body' — the hermeneutical rule for Jn 20:17 stated as metaphysics.
'From the base of his feet' — Origen's reductio: a walking God has audible footfalls in a paradise bigger than himself.
'Effluence' (ἀποῤῥοή) renders aporrhoē, the Wis 7:25 term for Wisdom's emanation — essence withdrawn, effluence shared.
title: The Father “in the heavens”

english: 'Hallowed be thy name.' When prayer sets forth something as not yet come to be, concerning which one prays — or, having obtained this, asks that it remain and be kept — it is plain, on the face of the words here, that we are commanded to say, in Matthew and in Luke, 'Hallowed be thy name,' as though the Father's name were not yet hallowed. And how, one might say, does a man deem it worthy that God's 'name' be hallowed, as though unhallowed? What the Father's 'name' is, and what hallowing it is, let us consider.

A 'name,' then, is a summary appellation, indicative of the proper quality of the named — as, say, some proper quality of Paul the apostle: one of his soul, whereby it is of such a sort; another of his mind, whereby he is contemplative; another of his body, whereby it is of such a sort. What is peculiar in these qualities, then, and unconfused toward another — for there is no other in being exactly unvarying from Paul — is declared by the appellation 'Paul.' But in men, whose proper qualities change, as it were, the names too are soundly changed according to Scripture: for when the quality of 'Abram' changed, he was called 'Abraham'; and when Simon's did, he was named 'Peter'; and the persecutor of Jesus, 'Saul,' was addressed as 'Paul.' But with God — who is himself unchangeable and unalterable, ever the same — there is ever one, as it were, name upon him too: the 'I am' spoken in Exodus, if we may so speak. Since, then, we all suppose something concerning God, conceiving whatever notions about him — but all do not grasp what he is (for rare, and, if one must say so, rarer than the rare, are those who grasp his holiness in all things) — we are fittingly taught that our inner conception of God become holy, that we may see his holiness: creating and providing and judging and choosing and forsaking, accepting and rejecting, counting worthy of honor and chastising each according to worth.

For in these and like things, if I may so speak, is characteristically stamped God's proper quality — which I take to be called God's 'name' in the Scriptures: in Exodus, 'Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain' (Matthew 6:9); in Deuteronomy, 'Let my utterance wait as rain; let my words come down as dew, as shower upon grass and as snowfall upon herb: for I have called the name of the Lord' (Exodus 3:14); in the Psalms, 'They shall remember thy name in every generation and generation.' (Exodus 20:7) For he who misfits his conception of God takes 'the name of the Lord God' 'in vain'; and he who can utter rain that co-works with his hearers for the fruit-bearing of their souls, and bring forth words like dew — comforting words — and by the rush of well-built speeches bring upon his hearers most profitable rain or most useful snowfall — can do these things for this reason. Having conceived this, he calls upon himself the one who begs God, who perfects, the true giver of the things aforesaid. And everyone who makes plain the things concerning God reminds rather than teaches — even if he seems to hear from someone or thinks he finds the mysteries of godliness.

As, then, the pray-er must here understand to ask that God's 'name' be hallowed, so in the Psalms 'Let us exalt his name together' is said — with the prophet commanding, in all harmony, in the same mind and the same judgment, to arrive beforehand at the true and lofty knowledge of God's proper quality. For this is exalting God's 'name' 'together': when one, having received of divinity's effluence by conceiving from God and getting mastery over his enemies, gladdened at a fall they cannot effect, exalts the very power of God of which he has shared. Which is declared in the twenty-ninth Psalm through 'I will exalt thee, O Lord, for thou hast upheld me, and hast not gladdened my enemies over me.' (Deuteronomy 32:2) And one exalts God by consecrating him a house in oneself — since even the psalm's title runs thus: 'A Psalm of a song, for the dedication of the house, of David.' (Psalm 44:18 (LXX))

Further, concerning the 'Hallowed be thy name' and its sequels, spoken in the imperative character, we must say that the translators continually used imperatives for optatives — as in the Psalms, 'Let lying lips be made dumb, that speak iniquity against the righteous,' (Psalm 33:4 (LXX)) for 'may they be made dumb'; and 'Let the moneylender search out all his goods; let him have no helper' (Psalm 29:1 (LXX)) — in the hundred-and-eighth, concerning Judas. For the whole psalm is a petition concerning Judas, that such things befall him. But Tatian, not observing that the 'let it be' does not always signify the optative but sometimes the imperative too, most impiously supposed concerning the God who said 'Let there be light' — that he prayed rather than commanded the light to come to be. Since, as that man impiously conceives, 'God was in darkness.' To him we must say: how will he take the 'Let the earth bring forth the herb of grass,' (Psalm 30:1 title (LXX)) and 'Let the water below heaven be gathered,' (Genesis 1:3,9,11,20,24) and 'Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls,' (Psalm 44:18) and 'Let the earth bring forth the living soul' (Psalm 33:4)? Does he pray, for the sake of standing firmly, that 'the water below heaven be gathered into one gathering' (Psalm 29:1)? Or does he pray, to share in what sprouts from earth, the 'Let the earth bring forth'? And what like need have the water creatures and winged and land creatures as the need of light, that he should pray concerning them too? And if, on his own showing, praying about these things — spoken with imperative appellations — is absurd, why not say the like concerning the 'Let there be light': that it was spoken not optatively but imperatively? I deemed it necessary, since a prayer spoken in imperative voices has come up, to recall his misreadings — for the sake of those deceived who have received his impious teaching, of whom we ourselves once had experience.
notes_covered: Name as proper-quality summary; Abram/Peter/Paul renamings
Holy inner conception of judging/providing God
Personal note: we once experienced deception
translator_notes: 'Summary appellation' (κεφαλαιώδης προσηγορία): a name compresses proper quality; Paul/Abram examples kept concrete.
'Rarer than the rare' — Origen's superlative for those grasping God's holiness in all his judgings and forsakings.
'Misreadings' (παρεκδοχαί): Tatian's optative-imperative confusion; the personal 'we ourselves once had experience' kept verbatim — Origen's convert past.
title: “Hallowed be thy name”

english: 'Thy kingdom come.' The 'kingdom of God,' according to the word of our Lord and Savior, 'comes not with observation,' (1 Corinthians 15:50–55) 'nor shall they say: Lo here, or lo there' (Luke 17:20–21) — but 'the kingdom of God is within' us ('for the word is very nigh, in our mouth and in our heart' (Deuteronomy 30:14)). So it is plain that the one who prays for God's kingdom to come rightly prays concerning God's kingdom in himself — that it rise and bear fruit and be perfected. For every saint is ruled by God and obeys God's spiritual laws, dwelling in himself as in a well-ordered city — with the Father present to him, and Christ co-reigning with the Father in the perfected soul, according to the saying I recalled not long ago: 'We will come to him and make our abode with him.' (John 14:23) And I suppose God's kingdom is recognized as the blessed state of the ruling faculty and the ordered rank of wise reasonings, and Christ's kingdom as the progressive words, saving to their hearers, and the works of righteousness performed, and of the other virtues — for the Son of God is Word and Righteousness. But every sinner is tyrannized by the 'ruler of this age,' since every sinner is owned by the present evil age, not offering himself to him who 'gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from the present evil age' (Galatians 1:4) — and he 'delivers' 'according to the will of our God and Father,' (Romans 6:12) according to what is said in Galatians. And he who is tyrannized by this ruler of the age is ruled by sin by the voluntariness of his sinning. That is why Paul orders us no longer to submit when sin wills to rule us, commanding through these words: 'Let not sin, then, reign in your mortal body, to obey its lusts.' (1 Corinthians 12:8; 13:9–12)

But someone will say, to both — both the 'Hallowed be thy name' and the 'Thy kingdom come' — that if the pray-er prays to be heard, and is heard at some point, then plainly at some point God's 'name' shall be hallowed for someone, as aforesaid, and God's 'kingdom' shall stand in him. And if these things shall be his, how will he still becomingly pray concerning things present as though not present, saying 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come' (Philippians 3:13)? And if so, will there ever be a time when it is not becoming to say 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come' (1 Corinthians 15:24–28, 50–55)? We must say to this that, as one who prays to obtain a 'word of knowledge' and a 'word of wisdom' becomingly prays concerning these things always — always receiving, as he is heard, more contemplations of 'wisdom' and 'knowledge,' yet knowing 'in part' whatever at present he can hold, with the perfect, which annuls 'the partial,' 'then' to be revealed, when mind without sense assails the realities 'face to face' — so the perfect, both of hallowing God's 'name' in each of us and of his kingdom standing in him, cannot be unless the perfect 'come' also concerning 'knowledge' and 'wisdom' — and perhaps concerning the other virtues too. We journey toward perfection if we 'press toward the things before, forgetting the things behind.' (2 Corinthians 6:14–15) To God's kingdom in us, then, the summit shall stand as we advance without ceasing — when what the Apostle said is fulfilled: that Christ, when all enemies are subjected to him, 'shall deliver the kingdom to God the Father, that God may be all in all.' (Colossians 3:5) That is why, praying 'without ceasing,' with a disposition made godlike by the Word, we say to our Father in the heavens: 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come.' (Galatians 5:22)

But concerning God's kingdom this too must be examined: that as there is no 'partnership of righteousness with lawlessness,' (Psalm 110:1) nor 'fellowship of light with darkness,' nor 'concord of Christ with Beliar' — so the kingdom of sin cannot co-exist with God's kingdom. If, then, we wish to be ruled by God, let 'sin in no way reign in our mortal body,' (1 Corinthians 13:9–12) nor let us obey its commands, when it calls our soul to 'the works of the flesh' and things foreign to God. But 'mortifying our members on earth,' let us bear the fruits 'of the Spirit,' that as in a spiritual 'paradise' the Lord may walk in us, ruling us alone with his Christ — seated 'at his right hand' in us, from whom we pray to receive spiritual 'power' — and seated, 'until' all his enemies in us become 'the footstool of his feet,' and every principality and authority and power be annulled from us. For these things can come to be in each of us, and the last enemy be annulled — death — so that in us too it be said by Christ: 'O death, where is thy sting? O Hades, where is thy victory?' (1 Corinthians 15:24–28) Now, then, let our 'corruptible put on' holiness in continence and all purity, and 'incorruption' — and our 'mortal' be clothed, death being annulled, with the Father's 'incorruption' — so that, ruled by God, we may already be in the goods of regeneration and resurrection.

'Made godlike by the Word' (θεοποιουμένης): disposition deified — theosis vocabulary kept literal.
title: “Thy kingdom come”

english: 'Thy will be done, as in heaven, also upon earth.' (Matthew 6:10) Luke, after the 'Thy kingdom come,' passed over these words in silence and goes on: 'Our daily bread give us day by day.' (Ephesians 6:12) So let us examine the words we set first, as lying in Matthew alone, in sequence with what went before. Still being 'on earth,' those who pray conceive that God's 'will' has come to be 'in heaven' among all the dwellers in heaven; and we pray that God's 'will' may come to be in us, who are 'still on earth,' in all things as with them. Which shall happen when we do nothing against his 'will.' And when God's 'will' — 'as in heaven' — is accomplished in us who are 'on earth,' we who are likened to those in the heavens, having borne, like them, 'the image of the heavenly,' (1 Corinthians 15:48–49) shall inherit the 'kingdom of the heavens' (Job 40:19 (LXX)) — we who pray on earth that we, having become 'in heaven,' be likened to them.

But according to Matthew alone, the 'as in heaven and on earth' (Luke 10:18) can be taken in common — so that what is enjoined upon us to say in prayer runs thus: 'Hallowed be thy name' (1 Corinthians 15:50) 'as in heaven and on earth' (1 Corinthians 15:48–50); 'Thy kingdom come' 'as in heaven and on earth' (Job 40:19); 'Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth.' (Isaiah 34:5) For God's 'name' has been hallowed among those 'in heaven,' and God's 'kingdom' has stood in them, and God's 'will' has come to be in them — all of which is lacking to us who are 'on earth,' but can come to be ours as we make ourselves worthy to obtain God's hearing concerning all these things.

But someone may ask, saying 'Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth' (1 Corinthians 6:17): how has God's 'will' come to be 'in heaven,' where 'the spiritual hosts of wickedness' are, on account of which God's 'sword shall be drunk' 'in heaven'? And if we so pray that God's 'will' come to be 'on' 'earth' as it is done 'in heaven,' might we unawares be praying that contrary things also remain 'on earth' — since these too come from heaven — with many base things coming to be 'on earth' through the inferior 'spiritual hosts of wickedness' that are 'in the heavenly places'? One who allegorizes heaven, saying it is Christ, and earth the church — for who is so 'a throne' of the Father as Christ? And what 'footstool of God's feet' as the church? — will easily loose the questions, saying each member of the church must so receive the paternal 'will' as Christ received it — who came to do his Father's 'will' and perfected it all. For it is possible, joined to him, to become 'one spirit' with him, thereby receiving the 'will' as one: as it is perfected 'in heaven,' so may it be perfected 'also on earth.' For 'he who is joined to the Lord,' according to Paul, 'is one spirit.' And I suppose this interpretation will prove not contemptible to one who considers it more exactly.

But one who opposes it will set beside it what was said at the end of this Gospel, after the resurrection, by the Lord to the eleven disciples: 'All authority has been given me, as in heaven, also on earth.' (Matthew 28:18) For having authority over those 'in heaven' — he says he has received in addition that 'on earth': those 'in heaven' having been enlightened even before by the Word, and at the 'consummation of the age' those 'on earth' too, through the authority given to the Son of God, imitating the things accomplished 'in heaven,' over which the Savior received authority. As it were, then, through our prayers he wishes to take those discipled to him as co-workers with the Father — that, as the things 'in heaven' are subjected to truth and the Word, so the things 'on earth,' set right through the authority he received 'as in heaven and on earth,' may bring the ruled to a blessed end. And one who calls the Savior heaven and earth the church — 'the firstborn of all creation,' in whom the Father rests as upon a throne, calling him heaven — would find the 'man' whom he put on, made his own by that power through 'humbling himself' and becoming 'obedient unto death,' saying after the resurrection the 'All authority has been given me, as in heaven and on earth' (Colossians 1:15) — the authority 'in heaven,' as of the things indwelling the Only-begotten, received by the man according to the Savior, that he may share it with him, mingled with his divinity and united to him.

But since the second interpretation does not yet loose the difficulties concerning how God's 'will' is 'in heaven,' with the spiritual hosts 'of wickedness' 'in the heavenly places' wrestling against those 'on earth' — from that side it will be possible to loose the question thus: that, as it is not by place but by choice that one 'on earth,' having his 'citizenship in heaven' and treasuring 'in heaven,' with his heart 'in heaven,' bearing 'the image of the heavenly,' is no longer 'of the earth' nor of the 'below' 'world,' but of heaven and of the better, 'heavenly' 'world' beyond this — so too the 'spiritual hosts of wickedness' still lingering 'in the heavenly places,' having their 'citizenship on earth,' plotting against men through what they wrestle, treasuring on earth, bearing 'the image of the earthy' — 'he who is the beginning of the Lord's creation, made to be mocked by the angels' — are not heavenly nor in the heavens, because of their wretched disposition. When, then, it is said 'Thy will be done, as in heaven, also on earth,' (Philippians 2:8) those must not be reckoned to be 'in heaven' at all — having fallen in mind with him who fell 'from heaven' 'like lightning.'

And perhaps, when our Savior commands that we must pray that the Father's 'will' come to be 'as in heaven' 'so also on earth,' he does not at all command that our prayers concern those in the place 'above,' that they be likened to those in the heavenly place. His injunction of prayer is, for one who wishes all things 'on earth' — that is, the worse things, made like to earthly things — to be likened to the better, to all who have 'their citizenship in heaven,' who have all become heaven. For the sinner, wherever he is, is 'earth' — who, unless he repent, shall come to his kindred earth. But he who does God's 'will' and disobeys none of the saving spiritual laws is heaven. Whether, then, we are still 'earth' through sin, let us pray that God's 'will' extend over us too, setting right, as it already reached those before us who are heaven or were heaven; or whether we are reckoned by God no longer earth but heaven already, let us ask that 'on earth' too, as in 'heaven' — I mean, among the worse — God's 'will' be fulfilled, unto the heaven-making, if I may so speak, of earth, so that earth be earth no longer, but all things become heaven. For if God's 'will,' as 'in heaven' in the senses interpreted, come to be 'also on earth,' earth shall not remain earth. As if I spoke more plainly on another example: if God's 'will,' as it has come to be upon the temperate, so come to be also upon the intemperate, the intemperate shall be temperate; or as God's 'will' has come to be upon the righteous, if it so come to be also upon the unrighteous, the unrighteous shall be righteous. That is why, if God's 'will,' as it has come to be 'in heaven,' come to be 'also on earth,' we shall all be heaven — with the unprofitable flesh and its kindred blood unable to inherit 'God's kingdom,' but to be said to inherit if they 'change from flesh and earth and dust and blood to the heavenly substance.' (Philippians 3:20)
translator_notes: 'Taken in common' (ἀπὸ κοινοῦ): the 'as in heaven and on earth' distributed across all three petitions — kept as grammatical term.
'He who is the beginning of the Lord's creation, made to be mocked by the angels' — Job's leviathan (LXX 40:19/41) identified with the earthy powers.
'Heaven-making' (οὐρανοποίησιν): Origen's coined end — earth heavened; kept as coinage.
title: “Thy will be done”

english: 'Give us this day our daily bread' — or as Luke has it, 'Our daily bread give us day by day.' (Matthew 6:11) Since some suppose these words are said concerning bodily food — that we pray for it — it is worth removing their false opinion by these arguments and setting forth the truth concerning the daily bread. We must say to them: how could he who says we must ask heavenly and great things — when neither is the bread dispensed into our flesh heavenly, nor is the request concerning it a great petition — as it were forgetting what he taught, command the address of an entreaty to the Father concerning an earthly and small thing?

But we, following him as teacher, shall set forth at greater length the teachings concerning this bread. He says in John, to those who came to Capernaum seeking him: 'Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.' (John 6:26–58) For he who ate 'of' the loaves blessed by Jesus and was filled with them rather seeks to grasp the Son of God more exactly, and hastens to him. That is why he well commands, saying: 'Labor not for the food that perishes, but for the food that abides unto eternal life, which the Son of Man shall give you.' (Psalm 107:20) And when his hearers asked and said, 'What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?' (Exodus 34:28) Jesus answered and said to them: 'This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.' (John 1:14) And God sent 'his Word and healed them,' as written in the Psalms — plainly, those who were sick. With this Word, those who believe work 'the works of God' — which are food abiding unto eternal life. And 'my Father,' he says, 'gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.' (1 Corinthians 3:2) And true bread nourishes the 'true' 'man' — made 'after the image of God' — who, nourished, becomes 'after the likeness' 'of him who created.' And what is more nourishing to the soul than the Word? What more precious to the mind that holds her than God's wisdom? What more fitting to the rational nature than truth?

But if someone objects to this, saying he would not teach us to ask for the daily bread as for another bread distinct from himself, let him hear that in John too, in one place he discourses of it as of another beside himself, in another as being himself the bread: as of another, in these words — 'Moses gave you not the bread from heaven,' (Hebrews 5:12–14) 'not the true,' 'but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven' (Romans 14:2); as of himself, he says to those who said to him, 'Evermore give us this bread': 'I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst.' (Proverbs 15:17) And after a little: 'I am the (living) bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eat of this bread, he shall live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.' (Amos 8:11)

And since every food is called bread according to Scripture — as plain from its being recorded of Moses that 'bread he did not eat for forty days, and water he did not drink' (Exodus 19:5) — and varied and diverse is the nourishing Word, since not all can be nourished, by firmness and vigor, on the divine lessons — therefore, wishing to present athletic food suited to the more perfect, he says: 'The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.' (Genesis 3:22) And after a little: 'Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. He who chews my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him at the last day. For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. He who chews my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, I too live by the Father; and he who chews me, he too shall live by me.' (Proverbs 3:18) And this is the 'true' 'food' — the 'flesh' of Christ, which, being 'Word,' became 'flesh,' according to the saying 'And the Word became flesh.' And when we chew and drink him, he 'tabernacled in us'; and when he is dispensed, 'we beheld his glory' is fulfilled. 'This is the bread that came down from heaven — not as the fathers ate and died; he who chews this bread shall live forever.' (Psalm 78:25)

But Paul, discoursing to 'babes' and Corinthians walking 'after man,' says: 'Milk I gave you to drink, not food; for you were not yet able. But neither even now are you able; for you are still carnal.' (Genesis 18:6) And in Hebrews: 'And you have come to need milk, not solid food. For everyone who shares milk is without experience of the word of righteousness — for he is a babe. But solid food is for the perfect, who by habit have their senses trained to discern good and evil.' (Revelation 3:20) And I take even the 'One believes he may eat all things, but the weak eats herbs' (Matthew 3:7) to be said by him principally not of bodily foods but of God's words that nourish the soul: the most faithful and most perfect can partake of all — whom he indicates through the 'One believes he may eat all things' — while the weaker and more imperfect begins with simpler lessons, which do not strongly impart vigor — whom, wishing to mark him, he calls 'the weak eats herbs.'

And I take what is said with Solomon in the Proverbs to teach that he who, through simplicity, cannot hold the more vigorous and greater doctrines — yet does not think amiss — is better than the readier, sharper man who charges more greatly upon realities but does not make plain the word of the peace and harmony of all. The wording runs thus: 'Better a portion of herbs with friendship and grace than a calf from the stall with hatred.' (Psalm 74:13–14) Often, at any rate, we have welcomed a private and simpler feast with a good conscience — entertained by those who could set nothing more before us — rather than loftiness of words raised 'against the knowledge of God,' proclaiming with great plausibility a doctrine foreign to the Father who gave 'the law and the prophets,' the Father of our Lord Jesus. That our soul, then, may not sicken for lack of foods, nor die to God 'by famine of the Lord's word,' let us ask of the Father the living bread — who is the same as the daily — persuaded by our teacher and Savior, believing and living more rightly.

But what the 'daily' is must now be considered. And first know this: that the word 'daily' (epiousios) has been named by no Greek, neither of the wise nor in common private usage — but seems coined by the evangelists. At any rate Matthew and Luke agreed upon it, bringing it forth nowise differing. The translators of the Hebrew did the like in other cases too. For what Greek ever used the appellation 'give ear' (enotizou), or the 'be eared' (akoutistheti) for 'receive with ears and make hearing'? Like the appellation 'daily' (epeousion) is what stands written with Moses, spoken by God: 'But you shall be to me' 'a peculiar people' (periousios). And each word seems to me made from 'substance' (ousia) — the one declaring the bread that contributes toward substance, the other signifying the people concerned with substance and sharing in it.

Now 'substance,' properly, is conceived by those who say the subsistence of the incorporeal is prior: after the incorporeal — things stably having being, admitting neither addition nor suffering subtraction (for this is peculiar to bodies, about which increase and wasting occur, since they are fluent, needing the incoming sustainer that nourishes; if more comes in seasonally than flows away, increase occurs; if less, decrease; and perhaps some receive the incoming thing not at all, in unmixed, if I may so speak ... ). But by those who deem substance consequent, with bodies prior, its definitions are these: substance is either the first matter of beings, and that from which beings come; or the matter of bodies, and that from which bodies come; or of named things, and that from which named things come; or the first substrate without quality; or what pre-subsists for beings; or what receives all changes and alterations, itself unaltered in its own ratio; or what abides through all alteration and change. On their view substance is both qualityless and unfigured in its own ratio — having no appointed magnitude either — but is set under every quality like a ready place. And 'qualities' they ordinarily call activities and makings — wherein happenings and relations turn out to be; for they say substance shares in none of these in its own ratio, but is ever inseparable from one of them by affection — no less receptive of all the maker's activities, as he makes and changes. For the tone connate with it, pervading through all of every quality, is the cause of the economies about it. Through wholes, then, they call it changeable and through wholes divisible, and say all substance can be mingled with all — united, however.

But since, inquiring concerning substance on account of the 'daily bread' and the peculiar people, we said these things to discern what substance signifies — and bread in what went before was intelligible, which we had to ask — substance akin to the bread must necessarily be conceived: that as bodily bread, dispensed, passes into the body of the nourished and into its substance, so the 'living' bread, 'come down from heaven,' dispensed into mind and soul, may share its own power with the one who offered himself to nourishment from it. And so shall be what we ask: 'daily bread.' And again: as, according to the 'quality' of the 'food' — whether 'solid' and suited to athletes, or milky and herby — the nourished comes to be in diverse power, so it follows that, as God's Word is becomingly given — whether as milk to babes, or as herbs to the sick in season, or as flesh to contenders in season — each of the nourished, by the analogy of the Word to which he offered himself, can do this or that, and become this or that. Yet there is a deemed food that is poisonous, and another that makes sick, and another that cannot even be dispensed — all of which must by analogy be transferred to the diversities of deemed nourishing lessons. Daily bread, then, is what is most fitting to the rational nature and most akin to substance itself — procuring at once health and good habit and strength for the soul, and sharing its own immortality (for God's Word is immortal) with the one who eats it.

This daily bread, then, seems to me called by another name in Scripture 'the tree of life' — toward which he who stretches 'his hand' and takes from it 'shall live forever.' And by a third name this 'tree' is called God's 'wisdom' with Solomon, in these words: 'She is a tree of life to all who cling to her, and safe as upon the Lord to those who lean.' (Genesis 19:37–38) And since angels too are nourished by God's wisdom — empowered, from contemplation in truth with wisdom, to perform their own works — it is said in the Psalms that angels too are nourished, with men of God — Hebrews, as they are called — sharing with the angels, and as it were feasting with them. Such is the 'bread of angels man ate.' For let our mind not be so poor as to suppose the angels, who ever partake, are nourished by some bodily bread — the storied bread that came down from heaven upon those who left Egypt — with the Hebrews sharing this same bread with the angels, God's ministering spirits.

It is not untimely, as we seek the 'daily bread' and the 'tree of life' and God's wisdom — the common food of holy men and angels — to attend also to the three men recorded in Genesis, brought down with Abraham and partaking of three measures of 'fine flour' kneaded into loaves: lest these things be said barely tropically, since the saints can at times share intelligible and rational food not only with men but even with diviner powers — whether for their benefit or to display what most nourishing things they have been able to procure for themselves — with the angels rejoicing and nourished in such display, and becoming readier to co-work in every way and to breathe together thereafter toward the grasp of more and greater things, upon the nourishing lessons furnished beforehand to the rest — he having gladdened and, if I may so speak, nursed them. It is no wonder if a man nourishes angels — when even Christ confesses he stands at the 'door' and knocks, that, entering with the one who opened to him, he may sup 'with him' from that one's goods, and afterwards himself share his own with the one who first feasted the Son of God, according to his own power.

Of the daily bread, then, he who partakes, strengthening his 'heart,' becomes a son of God; but he who shares in the 'dragon' is no other than the intelligible Ethiopian — changing, through the dragon's ... , even himself into a serpent — so that, reproached by the Word, even if he says he wishes to be baptized, he hears: 'Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?' (Matthew 28:15) And David says this concerning the dragon's body feasted upon by the Ethiopians: 'Thou didst crush the heads of the dragons upon the water; thou didst break the serpent's head in pieces; thou gavest him for food to the Ethiopian peoples.' But if it is no absurdity — with the Son of God substantially subsisting, and the Opponent also subsisting — that each becomes food, one to this one, one to that — why do we hesitate to accept, for all powers better and worse, and for men, that each of us can be nourished from all these? At any rate Peter, about to share with the centurion Cornelius and those gathered with him in Caesarea, and after this to share God's words with the nations too, sees 'heaven opened' and a 'vessel let down by four beginnings,' (Psalm 95:7) 'wherein were all the quadrupeds and creeping things and wild beasts of the earth' (Psalm 90:4) — and is bid 'rise,' sacrifice, and eat. And when, begging off, he said, 'Thou knowest that never did common or unclean enter my mouth,' (Hebrews 13:8) he is ordered to 'call no man common or unclean' — since what God cleansed Peter must not make common. For the saying runs: 'What God cleansed, make thou not common.' (Hebrews 10:1) So the clean food and the unclean, distinguished in the Mosaic law under names of many animals, referring to the diverse characters of the rationals, teaches that these are nourishing to us, these contrariwise — until God, cleansing all, makes all nourishing, or those 'from every nation.'

With these things so, and so great a difference of foods, one beyond all those named is the daily bread — concerning which we must pray to be counted worthy of it, and, nourished by the Word, who 'in the beginning' is 'toward God,' to be made godlike. But someone will say the 'daily' (epiousion) is formed from 'coming upon' (epienai) — so that we are commanded to ask the bread proper to the coming age, which God, taking beforehand, may already grant us: so that what is, as it were, to be given tomorrow be given us 'today' — 'today' taken of the present age, 'tomorrow' of the coming. But since the former interpretation is better, so far as I am judge, let us examine what lies beside it: the 'today' with Matthew, or the 'day by day' written with Luke. It is the custom in many places of Scripture to call the whole age 'today' — as 'this is the father of the Moabites unto this day,' (Hebrews 9:26) and 'this is the father of the Ammonites unto this day,' (Ephesians 2:7) and 'this saying was spread abroad among the Jews unto this day,' (Ephesians 3:20) and in the Psalms, 'Today, if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts.' (1 Corinthians 2:9) And with Jesus it is said most plainly thus: 'Depart not from the Lord in the today's days.' And if 'today' is this whole age, perhaps 'yesterday' is the age gone by. Which we have taken to be said in the Psalms and with Paul in Hebrews: in the Psalms thus — 'A thousand years in thy sight are as the day of yesterday, which is past' (1 Corinthians 3:21–22) (whatever the famed millennium is, likened to the 'yesterday' day, differing from the 'today'); and with the Apostle it is written: 'Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, the same, and unto the ages.' And it is no wonder that to God the whole age has the ratio of one day with us — I suppose, of even less.

And it must be examined whether the words of the feasts recorded by 'days' or 'months' or 'seasons' or 'years' or 'assemblies' refer to ages. For if 'the law has a shadow of the coming things,' the many sabbaths must be a 'shadow' of many days, and the new moons, occurring through temporal intervals — I know not with what moon attending what sun they are performed. And if the first 'month,' and the tenth day 'unto the fourteenth,' and the feast of unleavened from the fourteenth 'unto the twenty-first,' contain a 'shadow of coming things' — 'who is wise, and' to such degree a 'friend' of God, as to see, of more months, the first, and its tenth day, and what follows? And what need to speak of the feast of seven weeks of days, and of the seventh month — whose new moon is a day 'of trumpets,' and whose tenth day is a day 'of atonement' — known to the God alone who legislated them? And who has so held the mind of Christ as to grasp the seventh years of the Hebrew slaves' freedom, and the 'release' of debts, and rest from tilling the holy land? And there is one higher than the feast through seven years, called Jubilee — which, even to imagine in part, or to grasp plainly that its laws shall be fulfilled as true, belongs to none except the one who contemplated the Father's counsel concerning the ordinance in all the ages, according to his 'unsearchable' 'judgments' and his untraceable ways.

Often it came upon me to wonder, comparing two apostolic sayings, how it is the 'consummation of the ages,' at which Jesus 'has been manifested for the annulling of sins' — if ages are to come after this one. The sayings run thus: in Hebrews, 'But now once, at the consummation of the ages, he has been manifested, for the annulling of sins through his sacrifice'; in Ephesians, 'that in the coming ages he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us.' Pondering such greatness, I suppose that, as the last month is the consummation of the year — after which another month's beginning sets in — so perhaps, with many ages completing, as it were, a year of ages, the present age is the consummation, after which certain coming ages shall set in, whose beginning is the coming age — and in those coming ages God shall display the riches 'of his grace in kindness' — with the most sinful, even the blasphemer against the Holy Spirit, held fast by sin in the whole present age, and from the beginning to the end, to be dispensed in the coming age afterward — how, I know not.

He, then, who saw these things, and conceived in mind a week of ages — to contemplate a holy sabbatism — and a month of ages — to see God's holy new moon — and a year of ages — to understand together the year's feasts, when every 'male' must appear 'before the Lord God' — and the proportionate years of such ages — to grasp the holy seventh year — and seven sevens of ages — to hymn the so-great Lawgiver — having examined how he can fuss over the least portion of an hour of the day of so great an age, will do everything, that, made worthy by preparation here of obtaining the daily bread, he may receive it on the 'today' day — with the 'day by day' already becoming plain from what went before. For to the God who is from boundless to boundless, the one who prays concerning not only the 'today' but in a way the 'today' of the 'day by day' — from what he can contemplate — 'beyond all measure above what we ask or conceive' — shall be able to receive, if I may speak so hyperbolically, even 'what eye saw not' and 'what ear heard not' and 'what went not up upon man's heart.'

And these things too seem to me most necessary to examine, that both the 'today' be understood and the 'day by day,' when we pray that the 'daily bread' 'be given us' from his Father. But if in the last book we shall first examine the 'our' — since it is said not 'Give us this day our daily bread' but 'Our daily bread give us day by day' — yet we must examine how this bread is 'ours.' The Apostle teaches that 'whether life or death, or things present or things to come — all' are the saints'. Concerning which there is no need to speak at present.

english: 'And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors' (Matthew 6:12) — or as Luke has it, 'And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us.' (Romans 13:7–8) Concerning debts, the Apostle says: 'Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute, fear to whom fear, tax to whom tax, honor to whom honor. Owe no one anything, except to love one another.' (1 Samuel 2:25) We owe, then — holding certain duties — not only in giving, but in gentle speech too, and in certain works; and we owe a certain disposition toward them. These debts we either pay, by performing what the divine law commands, or, by despising the wholesome word, not paying, we remain in owing.

The like must be conceived for debts toward brothers — both those reborn with us in Christ by the word of godliness, and those of our womb or our father. There is a debt toward citizens too, and another common one toward all men — toward strangers in particular, and in particular toward those of a father's age — and another toward some, whom it is reasonable to honor as sons or as brothers. He who does not see that what is owed to brothers is performed remains a debtor of what he did not do. And he — if, when men cast upon us some of our failings, from the philanthropic spirit of wisdom — the debt grows greater. But we owe to ourselves too: to use the body thus — not to wear out the body's flesh by love of pleasure; and to bring this care to the soul, and make provision for the mind's keenness, and for speech, that it be stingless and useful and nowise idle. And when we do not do what is owed by us to ourselves, our liability becomes heavier.

And beyond all these, as God's 'workmanship' and creation, we owe him a certain disposition kept toward him, and love 'from the whole heart' 'and from the whole strength' 'and from the whole mind.' If we do not accomplish these, we remain debtors to God, sinning against the Lord. And who shall pray for us concerning these? 'For if a man sinning sin against a man, they shall pray for him; but if he sin against the Lord, who shall pray for him?' (Ephesians 4:30) — as Eli says in First Kingdoms. But with Christ having bought us with his own blood, we are debtors — as every slave is debtor to his buyer for so great a sum given for him. And we have a debt toward 'the Holy Spirit' too — paid when we grieve him not, 'whereby' we were 'sealed unto the day of redemption' — and, not grieving him, bear the fruits we are required to bear, with him present in us and quickening our soul. And if we know not exactly who is each one's angel, 'beholding' in the heavens the Father's 'face' — yet to each who oversees himself it becomes plain that to him too we are debtors of certain things. And if we are 'in a theater of the world and angels and men,' (Matthew 18:19 (angels)) know that, as in a theater one is debtor to say or do such things in sight of the spectators — which, if he do not, he is punished as having insulted the whole theater — so we owe 'to' the whole 'world' 'and' to all, angels and the race of men, the things we shall learn from wisdom if we will.

But apart from these more general debts, there is a debt of a widow cared for by the church, and another of a deacon, and another of a presbyter — and a bishop's debt is heaviest, exacted by the Savior of the whole church, and avenged if unpaid. And the Apostle named a common debt of man and wife, saying: 'Let the husband render the debt to the wife, and likewise the wife to the husband' (1 Corinthians 4:9) — adding, 'Defraud not one another.' And why must I say what readers of this writing can gather for themselves from what is said — how many debts, either not paying, we shall be held, or paying, be freed? Only, living in this life, there is no hour of night or day without owing.

But in owing, one either pays or keeps back the debt. In this life one can pay; one can also keep back. Some owe nothing to anyone; some, paying most, owe little; some, paying little, owe more; and perhaps there is one who, paying nothing, owes all. And he who pays all, so as to owe nothing, succeeds in this in time — needing forgiveness for former debts. Which forgiveness he who has been zealous, from some time, to become such as to owe nothing of what befalls him, as unpaid, may reasonably obtain. And these lawless activities, imprinted on the ruling faculty, become the 'handwriting against us' by which we shall be judged — as books, as it were, written by all hands, to be produced when 'we shall all stand before the tribunal' (1 Corinthians 7:3–5) 'of Christ, that each may receive the things through the body, according to what he did, whether good or bad.' (Colossians 2:14) To these debts belongs also what is said in Proverbs: 'Give not thyself for surety, ashamed of face; for if thou hast not whence to pay, they shall take thy mattress from under thy sides.' (2 Corinthians 5:10)

And if we owe to so many, then certainly some owe to us: some owe us as men, others as citizens, others as fathers, some as sons — and after these, wives to husbands as husbands, or friends to friends as friends. When, then, some of our many debtors behave more weakly concerning the payment of what is due to us, we shall do more humanely if we bear it with forgetfulness of wrongs toward them, remembering our own debts — how many we often passed by, not only toward men but toward God himself. For remembering that, being debtors, we did not pay but kept back, with time passing in which we should have done such things toward our neighbor, we shall be gentler toward those who owed even to us and did not pay the debt — especially if we forget not what was presumptuously done against the Divine by us, and the 'iniquity against the height' spoken by us, whether in ignorance of the truth or in displeasure at the circumstances befalling us.

But if we will not become gentler toward those indebted to us, we shall suffer what befell the one who forgave not his fellow-slave the 'hundred denarii' — who, forgiven according to the parable lying in the Gospel, was seized, and his master exacts the forgiven sums, saying to him: 'Wicked and slothful slave, oughtest thou not to have pitied thy fellow-slave, as I pitied thee? Cast him into prison, till he pay all that is owed.' (Proverbs 22:26–27) And the Lord adds to this: 'So also shall my heavenly Father do to you, if you forgive not each one his brother from your hearts.' (Matthew 18:23–35) Yet they say we must forgive the repentant among those who sinned against us, even if our debtor do this often: 'For,' he says, 'if seven times a day thy brother sin against thee,' (Luke 17:4) and seven times turn, saying 'I repent,' thou shalt forgive him. It is not we who are harsh toward the unrepentant — such are harsh to themselves: 'for he who casts off discipline hates himself.' (John 20:23) Yet even for such, healing must by every means be sought to come upon the wholly perverted — so as not even to perceive his own evils, but to be drunk with a drunkenness more deadly than 'from wine': the drunkenness from the stupor of wickedness.

But Luke, saying 'Forgive us our sins' — since sins are debts of debtors who owe and pay not — says the same as Matthew, who seems to give no place to one who wishes to forgive only repentant debtors, since the Savior legislated that we must add in prayer: 'For we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us.' (1 John 5:16) Yet we all have authority to forgive sins against us — plain from both the 'as we also forgive our debtors' and the 'for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us.' (Job 1:5) But he who is breathed upon by Jesus as the apostles were, and can be known 'by their fruits' as having received the Holy Spirit, and become spiritual by being led by the Spirit in the manner of a son of God for each thing to be done according to reason — forgives whatever God forgives, and retains the unhealable sins, serving, as the prophets did in speaking not their own things but the divine will's to God — so he too serves the God alone who has authority to forgive.

The voices in John's Gospel concerning the apostles' forgiveness run thus: 'Receive the Holy Spirit. Whosesoever sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whosesoever you retain, they are retained.' (Matthew 18:10) But if anyone takes these without examination, one might blame the apostles for not forgiving all, that all be forgiven — but retaining some sins, so that through them they are retained with God too. It is useful to take an example from the Law, to understand the forgiveness of men's sins wrought by men under God for men. The priests according to the Law are forbidden to offer sacrifice for certain sins, that the trespasses for which the sacrifices are made be forgiven. And surely the priest, having authority for the offering concerning involuntary or ... trespasses, does not already offer whole-burnt-offering and sin-offering for adultery or willful murder or any graver fall. So too the apostles, and those likened to the apostles — priests under the 'great' 'High Priest,' having received knowledge of God's healing — know, taught by the Spirit, for what they must offer sacrifices of sins, and when, and in what manner — and know for what they must not do this. At any rate the priest Eli, knowing his sons Hophni and Phinehas sinning, as able to co-work nothing toward forgiveness of sins for them, confesses despair that this shall be, through what he says: 'If a man sinning sin against a man, they shall pray for him; but if he sin against the Lord, who shall pray for him?'

I know not how some, permitting themselves things beyond priestly worth — perhaps not even exact about priestly knowledge — boast as able to forgive idolatries, adulteries, and fornications too — to loose, through their prayer for the daring, even the 'sin unto death.' For they do not read the 'There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should ask concerning it.' Nor must we pass over in silence most manly Job, offering sacrifice for his sons, saying: 'Lest my sons in their mind conceived evil against God' — for concerning doubtful cases, whether sin was sinned — and these not even reaching the lips — he offers the sacrifice.
